documents.title: Incidence, prevalence and nature of injuries in padel: a systematic review.
documents.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: It is unclear what the incidence, prevalence and nature of injuries are that can occur during playing padel. This study aimed to systematically review the incidence, prevalence and nature of injuries in padel.
METHOD: A literature search was performed up to December 2022 through MEDLINE Ovid, PubMed, Cochrane Library, SportsDiscus and CINAHL. Following database search, article retrieval and title and abstract screening, articles were assessed for eligibility against predefined criteria. Studies were assessed for methodological quality. Data on injuries' prevalence, incidence and nature of injuries were extracted, analysed and described in a descriptive statistical manner which did not include a pooling strategy as part of a formal meta-analysis.
RESULTS: Eight studies with 2022 participants were included (range of mean age: 31-57). The incidence rate was 3 injuries per 1000 hours of padel training and 8 injuries per 1000 matches of padel practice. The overall prevalence range was 40%-95%. The elbow was the most common anatomical site of injury, followed by the knee, shoulder and lower back. Tendinous and muscular injuries were the most reported injury types.
CONCLUSION: Injuries are common among padel players, with an incidence rate of 3 per 1000 hours of padel training and 8 per 1000 matches of padel practice-as based on limited literature. The overall prevalence range was 40%-95%. The elbow was the most frequently reported anatomical region concerning location injury distribution, and injuries were mainly of tendinous or muscular origin.

Moreover, it is unclear which type of injuries occur during this sport. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS This study adds new findings to the literature summarising the literature on padel injuries finding that injuries to the musculoskeletal system are relativeily common in padel. The most frequently located injury location was the elbow. As such, this study can function as a stepping stone towards preventive interventions for this sport specifically. Introduction Padel is a contemporary doubles racket sport that originated in Acapulco, Mexico in 1962. The sport follows a scoring system and rules similar to tennis, with two pairs of players competing against each other. However, the key distinction lies in the enclosed synthetic glass and metal court, allowing the ball to rebound off the lateral and back walls. The court measures 20 m×10 m and features a tennis-like net dividing it in half. Each half court includes two service boxes, marked by a service line positioned 6.95 m away from the net. These court specifications, along with the presence of walls, result in the following specific movements: fast-paced lateral movements, quick changes in direction and explosive movements towards the net. 1–3 Padel is a physically demanding sport that places specific physiological demands on players. To perform at their best, padel players need to possess a combination of physical attributes, including cardiovascular endurance, strength, power, agility, flexibility and mental resilience. 4 5 The sport is increasing in popularity with a steadily growing number of players and courts in more than 40 countries. 6 7 The potential dangers of playing padel have highlighted the need to better understand the incidence, prevalence and nature of injuries among recreational and professional athletes. 2 6 8 9 Although the popularity of padel has been growing exponentially, knowledge of the injury rates is limited. There is no consensus on the definition of injury provided by the International Padel Federation, which may cause misdiagnosis and under-reporting of injuries. Moreover, solely a handful of studies are available on the epidemiology and nature of injuries during padel. 6 10–12 The lack of reporting on injuries in padel within the scientific literature is a significant limitation that hinders our understanding of the sport’s injury landscape. The limited number of studies examining padel injuries restricts the availability of reliable and robust data on injury rates, mechanisms and associated factors. This knowledge gap undermines our ability to develop evidence-based injury prevention strategies, implement targeted interventions, and ultimately promote the safety and well-being of padel players. Therefore, this study aimed to systematically review the incidence, prevalence and nature of injuries occurring in this sport. The clinical relevance of this study relates to increasing insight into the epidemiology and type of injuries which will guide future research by building baseline data and inform the development of interventions for managing and preventing the reported injuries in this specific racket sport—as understanding the burden of the injury in this sport is the first step of the ‘Sequence of Prevention’ in creating targeted injury prevention strategies. 13 14 Materials and methods Registration and PE(C)O question This review was submitted for registration in the International Prospective Register of Systematic review on the 17 January 2023 and was accepted on the first of March 2023 with reference number CRD42023387984. Our PE(C)O 15 question was as follows: what are the incidence and prevalence rates as well as the nature of injuries (outcome(s)) in recreational and professional padel players (population) performing padel training or matches (exposure)? As there was no formal comparison group included, the C of the PECO was not included. Literature search strategy A systematic literature review was performed and reported according to the methodology of the 2020 Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses. 16 17 A comprehensive search of MEDLINE Ovid, PubMed, Cochrane Library, SportsDiscus and CINAHL databases was performed from inception to 17 December 2022, for potentially eligible articles. The following keywords were used: “padel”, “paddle tennis”, “paddle-tennis”, “injury” and “injuries”, including synonyms and MeSH terms. The full search strategy is outlined in online supplemental appendix 1 . Duplicates were subsequently removed. 10.1136/bmjsem-2023-001607.supp1 Supplementary data Study selection and eligibility criteria Two independent reviewers (JD and KSE) screened titles and abstracts using predefined criteria in Rayyan. 18 Subsequently, articles were screened for full text and included when they met the inclusion criteria. Discordant judgement in study inclusion was resolved by consensus discussion. In case of persistence of discussion, the senior author (BMP) was questioned whether to include or exclude the publication. One author searched the reference lists of all included studies to identify any other potential articles for inclusion. Studies were included if they reported incidence (injuries per unit of playing time), prevalence (fraction of injured players per reported time frame) or injury type (as the fraction of injuries) among a population of padel players participating in matches or training. Self-reported injury data and data on medical encounters (MEs) were included in this review as defined by Schwellnus et al . 19 Including self-reported injury data allows reporting on a broader scope of injuries as, in our opinion, not all padel players will report their injury to a medical professional. 20 No limit was placed on the geographical region of participation, age and sex of participants or publication date. Conference proceedings, editorials, commentaries, book chapters, opinion-based papers and reviews were excluded. Solely peer-reviewed articles were included. There was no limit on the language of the published studies: in case of inclusion of studies of language not being able to be understood by one of the authors, an external referent was requested to translate the manuscript. Methodological quality assessment All articles’ evidence level was assessed using the Oxford Center of Evidence-Based Medicine model. 21 The methodological quality of the studies was evaluated by two independent reviewers (JD and KSE) using the validated Critical Appraisal Tool for prevalence studies from the Joanna Briggs Institute to indicate the methodological quality of each study. 22 All studies were rated on nine criteria. Discrepancies between the two authors were resolved through consensus. Without consensus, the senior author (BMP) was requested to decide the methodological quality. Data extraction The following study characteristics were retrieved and extracted by one author: authors, year of publication and study design. Extracted data from the final selection of studies consisted of study design, year of study, population (sample size, age, sex), study location, the aim of the study, injury definition duration/follow-up, injury outcomes (incidence, prevalence, anatomical site, tissue type, specific diagnosis, severity). The extraction of the data was checked by the senior author (BMP). Data analysis Data analysis was performed by reporting variables extracted from the included studies. The incidence of injury was reported per 1000 hours of playing padel or per 1000 padel players per season with confidence intervals (CIs) (90% or 95% CI), while the period prevalence of injury was reported as the percentage of injured padel players per specific period. Self-calculated incidence and/or prevalence outcomes were used whenever hours of play were not reported as the primary outcome point. The injury frequency (n, %) was reported for anatomical site, tissue type and pathology-type/specific diagnosis categories. The frequency (n, %) and mean severity scores were reported for injury severity. Attempts were made to combine comparable data, however, in case of heterogeneous nature and reporting of data among the included studies, a formal meta-analysis would not be performed. Results Identification of studies After the removal of duplicates, the literature search resulted in 167 articles. After screening titles and abstracts, 15 articles were included for full-text screening. A total of eight articles 11 12 23–28 were included for analysis ( figure 1 ). Figure 1 PRISMA flow diagram. PRISMA, Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses. Study characteristics The publication dates and respective journals are presented in table 1 . A total of 2022 participants were studied. The mean age ranged from 31 to 57 and is shown in table 1 . Data on sex were available for all participants. The review included predominantly males (n=1516; 75%) vs 506 females (25%). Data were mainly collected in cross-sectional or retrospective studies. All 11 12 23–27 but one 28 study reported the data through a self-administered questionnaire. The difference in injury definitions and study designs as well as the heterogeneity of the included populations made it impossible to pool and compare results through a formal meta-analysis. Anatomical site of the injury Four out of eight (50%) studies reported the injury location as the upper or lower body (upper or lower extremities). Two (50%) studies reported the upper limbs/upper extremity as the most common injury location, 11 28 and two (50%) reported the lower limbs/lower extremity as the most common site of injury. 11 25 Five out of eight (63%) studies gave more detailed information and reported specific joints as injury location. 12 23–26 Five out of five (100%) studies reported the elbow as the most frequent injury site. However, one 26 study only analysed upper body injuries in amateur padel players. 12 23–26 Tissue type, pathology type and specific diagnosis Four out of eight (50%) studies reported the type of tissue or structure of the injuries. 11 25–27 In three 11 25 26 out of four (75%) studies, tendon injuries were most commonly reported, followed by muscle injuries, while muscle injuries were most common in the fourth study. 27 Specific pathology type and/or diagnosis were not mentioned in three out of eight (38%) studies. 26–28 The remaining five studies 11 12 23–25 mentioned a specific pathology type and/or diagnosis. It was not possible to extract one most common specific pathology and/or diagnosis. However, overall, tennis elbow (from now on referred to as common extensor tendinopathy, also known as lateral epicondylitis) was most frequently reported among the different studies. Injury severity Injury severity was reported by three studies out of eight studies (38%). 11 25 28 García-Fernández et al 25 classified the injury severity based on the classification of Pluim et al 29 : 30% of the injuries were minor, 28% were of moderate severity and severe or minimal injuries were not reported (hence the percentages potentially not adding up to 100%). Valério et al 28 also classified their injury severity with a similar system, with 65% of the injuries being mild, 19% being moderate and 16% being severe. Priego Quesada et al 11 assessed the injury severity with an associated time to recover: 53% of the athletes needed more than 1 month to fully recover from their injury, 13% of the athletes required to request a medical leave, while 9% required less than a week to recover from the injury. Training versus competition Injuries occurring during training or competition were reported in two studies. 27 28 Sánchez Alcaraz-Martínez et al 27 indicated that 58% of the lesions occurred during training, while 42% occurred during competition. Valério et al 28 stated that 44%–64% of the injuries occurred during competition, 20%–48% during padel training and 8%–16% during physical training. Discussion This study aimed to systematically review the literature on padel injuries to provide an overview of the characteristics, prevalence and nature of these injuries. Our results showed that injuries are common among padel players, with an incidence rate of 3 injuries per 1000 hours of padel training and 8 injuries per 1000 padel matches, and an overall prevalence ranging from 40% to 95%. This wide range may be due to differences in the population, the methods used to collect data and the definition of injury used in different studies. Comparing the incidence, prevalence and nature of injuries occurring during padel as summarised in this systematic review to other racquet sports can provide important information on the relative risk of injuries associated with this sport. This, is, however, to a certain extent difficult and methodologically inadequate due to the absence of (large) recent systematic reviews on the incidence/prevalence of injuries in other racquet sports, such as tennis, badminton and squash. For example, in a systematic review study by Pluim et al , 30 the reported injury incidence varied from 0.05 to 2.9 injuries per player per year, and per hour of play, the reported incidence ranged from 0.04 injuries per 1000 hours to 3.0 injuries per 1000 hours. In two more recent studies (which were not systematic reviews) on competitive adolescent tennis players, the prevalence of injury occurrence ranged from 1.2 to 2.8 injuries per 1000 hours played. 31 32 As these three studies included a mixture of both professional and non-professional athletes, comparing to padel injuries should be performed with caution. Concerning the occurrence of injuries per anatomic location, we could not determine from our analysis whether the lower extremities were more susceptible to injury than the upper extremities. Comparing this outcome in padel to the same outcome in tennis, Sell et al 33 studied the overall injury rates per 1000 match exposures and found a significantly higher injury rate in the lower extremities compared with the trunk and the upper extremities. A recent study of squash players, 76% of the injuries were lower-limb injuries. 34 In padel, the elbow was the most frequently reported site of injury, and common extensor tendinopathy (tennis elbow) was the most commonly reported specific pathology. Several studies have investigated the occurrence of elbow injuries in other racquet sports. Compared with other racquet sports, 33 padel appears to have a higher incidence of elbow injuries. This may be due to the specific nature of the sport, which involves a high number of overhead shots and repetitive movements that place strain on the elbow joint. An interesting finding from this review was the high proportion of tendon injuries reported in padel. This potentially has to do with the fact that the elbow (with the common extensor tendinopathy) was also the most frequently reported location of injuries, and, as such, may contribute to the high percentage of tendon injuries. The finding may be related to the fact that the elbow is suspect to high mechanical demands due to the continuous eccentric contractions occurring after hitting the ball in such a technical fashion to slow down the speed of the incoming ball as a tactical manoeuvre. Another reason for the high prevalence of the tendinous injuries could be that the padel racquet does not consist of stringing, so the tension is properly regulated during stroke hitting—as previously described by García-Fernández et al . 25 Other contributing explanations may be that the high number of overhead shots can place greater stress on the tendons of the elbow than on the muscular components around it, and that in padel double-handed backhands are rarely seen, as opposed to tennis. Concerning the severity of injuries, three studies 11 25 28 assessed this outcome. As the way of reporting injury severity varied among studies, no specific conclusions could be drawn. However, both Garcia and Valerio reported mostly mild to moderately severe injuries, with Valerio reporting 16% severe injuries. Moreover, comparing the severity of injuries occurring during padel to other racquet sports cannot be considered appropriate. The comparison is complex and depends on various factors—such as level of play, sex, age of players, etc. Therefore, it is essential to investigate further the nature and severity of injuries in racquet sports to develop effective injury prevention and management strategies. Concerning injuries occurring during practice or competition, one of the two studies concluded that more injuries occurred during competition than during practice, while one out of the two studies concluded the opposite. Here again, an appropriate comparison to other sports cannot be performed. We recognise the limitations of our study. First, most studies included in our review were conducted in Spain, which may limit the generalisability of our findings to other countries. Second, the definition of injury varied across studies, which may have resulted in underestimating or overestimating the true prevalence of injuries. Moreover, we did not include an analysis on the assessment of risk factors of injury occurrence in padel players, as there needs to be more data on this. Finally, the quality of the studies varied from relatively low-quality to moderate-quality studies, with some reporting limited information on the methods used to collect data or the population studied. Frequently reported reasons for scoring an ‘unclear’ or a ‘no’ as based on the Joanna Briggs Instiute’s critical appraisal checklist were the (in)adequate sample size and the unclarity concerning the adequateness of the response. As such, focus should be on improving these aspects around the methodological quality for future studies on the epidemiology of padel injuries. Though this review provided a comprehensive overview of the existing literature on padel injuries, there is still a need for further research in this area to improve the understanding of the nature and magnitude. Future studies should consider prospective designs, including larger sample sizes, longer follow-up periods and more standardised injury definitions and reporting methods. Additionally, more attention should be given to the role of individual player characteristics, playing style and environmental factors, as well as the effectiveness of injury prevention and rehabilitation programmes. A better understanding of the risk factors and prevention strategies of padel injuries could help promote this sport’s safe and sustainable practice. Conclusion Our results show that injuries are common among padel players, with an incidence rate of 3 injuries per 1000 hours of padel training and 8 injuries per 1000 padel matches, but based on limited literature. The career prevalence range was 60%–95% while the reported prevalence range over injuries occurring over the past 8–12 months was 40%–72%. The elbow was the most frequently reported injured anatomical region, and injuries mainly were of tendinous or muscular origin. documents.title: Exercise interventions for treating work-related complaints of the arm, neck or shoulder in adults.
documents.abstract: OBJECTIVES: This is a protocol for a Cochrane Review (intervention). The objectives are as follows: To assess the effects of exercise interventions for work-related complaints of the arm, neck or shoulder (CANS) in adults. The outcomes of interest are pain, function, work outcomes, adverse events, quality of life, healthcare use and injury recurrence.

The outcomes of interest are pain, function, work outcomes, adverse events, quality of life, healthcare use and injury recurrence. pmc-status-qastatus 0 pmc-status-live yes pmc-status-embargo no pmc-status-released yes pmc-prop-open-access yes pmc-prop-olf no pmc-prop-manuscript no pmc-prop-legally-suppressed no pmc-prop-has-pdf yes pmc-prop-has-supplement no pmc-prop-pdf-only no pmc-prop-suppress-copyright no pmc-prop-is-real-version no pmc-prop-is-scanned-article no pmc-prop-preprint no pmc-prop-in-epmc yes pmc-license-ref CC BY-NC New Background Description of the condition Work‐related upper limb disorders, repetitive strain injuries, cumulative trauma disorders, occupational overuse syndromes or work‐related complaints of the arm (including wrist, hand and fingers), neck or shoulder (CANS) are frequently used terms for disorders that develop as a result of repetitive movements, awkward postures and impact of external forces such as when operating vibrating tools ( Boocock 2009 ). Work‐related complaints can be divided into specific conditions with relatively clear diagnostic criteria and pathology, such as carpal tunnel syndrome, or non‐specific conditions, such as tension neck syndrome. Non‐specific conditions are usually defined by the location of complaint, with a pathophysiology that is less clearly defined or relatively unknown ( Staal 2007 ). In this review, we use CANS as a descriptor for work‐related upper‐limb musculoskeletal complaints. The use of the CANS classification was supported by a multidisciplinary Delphi study that provided a list of 23 specific CANS diagnoses and non‐specific CANS diagnoses ( Huisstede 2007 ). Specific diagnoses include: bursitis of the elbow, carpal tunnel syndrome, cervical disc hernia, complex regional pain syndrome, cubital tunnel syndrome, De Quervain’s disease, frozen shoulder, Guyon canal syndrome, instability of the elbow, instability of the shoulder, glenoid labral lesion, lateral epicondylitis, local arthritis of a joint of the upper extremities, medial epicondylitis, Oarsman’s wrist, radial tunnel syndrome, Raynaud’s phenomenon, rotator cuff tears, subacromial impingement syndrome/rotator cuff‐related shoulder pain, suprascapular nerve compression, biceps tendon tendinitis and trigger finger ( Huisstede 2007 ). People can also have non‐specific CANS where no specific diagnosis can be made ( Armstrong 1993 ), and where no pathological, neurological or radiological characteristics can be found to support the diagnosis of CANS ( Staal 2007 ). Non‐specific CANS includes non‐specific pain that is not listed as one of the 23 specific CANS diagnoses ( Huisstede 2007 ). Using CANS as a descriptor allows for the grouping of a number of upper‐limb complaints that facilitate comparisons ( Huisstede 2007 ). The aetiology of CANS is multifactorial and can vary between diagnoses ( Huisstede 2007 ). For example, carpal tunnel syndrome can be caused by repetitive hand movements with awkward postures (such as typing or using a computer mouse) and due to a swelling and narrowing of the synovial membrane of flexor tendons at the wrist, resulting in pain, weakness and numbness ( Padua 2023 ). Rotator cuff‐related shoulder pain can be caused by overhead repetitive movements of the arm (such as painting), which causes shoulder swelling, shoulder pain and weakness during arm movements ( Powell 2022 ). Work‐related CANS severely affect working populations worldwide. In the USA, the incidence of work‐related musculoskeletal disorders in the upper limb involving days away from work in private industries was 12.9/10,000 workers in 2020, with a median time away from work of 21 days ( U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics 2023 ). In the UK, in 2022, an estimated 1130/100,000 workers were affected by (self‐reported) work‐related musculoskeletal disorders, with the highest proportion of people affected by these being females aged 35 to 54 ( HSE 2023 ). The Labour Force Survey estimates that 6.9 million working days (full‐day equivalent) were lost in 2018/19 in the UK through musculoskeletal disorders, with 41% of disorders affecting the upper limbs or neck. Work‐related musculoskeletal disorders accounted for 29% of all lost working days; on average, each affected person took 14 days off work ( HSE 2023 ). Although the incidence of work‐related CANS is high, there may still be many unreported cases ( Kyung 2023 ). Description of the intervention This review evaluates exercise interventions. We define exercise as "... participation in physical activity that is planned, structured, repetitive and purposeful for the improvement or maintenance of a specific health condition (or disease)" ( Nicolson 2017 , pp. 1). Types of exercise interventions that are prescribed or performed in the treatment of CANS include any planned or structured activity that is done either by the person with CANS or with the assistance of someone else. Exercise interventions can be whole‐body or specific to a body part, and may include stretching (active, active‐assisted, passive), strengthening and endurance exercises, general strengthening and aerobic exercises, as well as specific exercise therapies such as proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation (PNF), Mensendieck training or Feldenkrais therapy. We describe our exercise intervention inclusion criteria in Types of interventions . How the intervention might work Exercise interventions are used widely in the treatment of CANS ( Staal 2007 ; Van Tulder 2007 ). It has been proposed that exercise can reduce pain, although the working mechanism at tissue level of most interventions is unclear. For example, muscles can weaken and shorten through prolonged postures during work ( Van Tulder 2007 ). The weakened and shortened muscles cause changes to joint torques, increasing stress on the weakened/shortened muscles and other muscle and bone structures, resulting in pain. Strengthening the weakened muscles can allow them to withstand the loads required ( Beneka 2014 ). Stretching shortened muscles can result in an increased range of motion, through increasing the length of soft tissues (such as muscles, tendons and ligaments) ( Beneka 2014 ; Harvey 2017 ). Both strengthening and lengthening muscles can reduce pain by normalising joint torques and reducing stress on muscles and bone structures, allowing for the appropriate stress and loads. Generally, exercise interventions aim to improve muscle strength, flexibility and range of motion, body mechanics and posture, and mental health and well‐being. A review of Cochrane reviews showed that exercise is frequently prescribed to people with pain and is rarely associated with worsening of pain ( Geneen 2017 ). Despite this, some studies show no changes in pain due to exercise interventions, while others show small, clinically insignificant differences in pain ( Geneen 2017 ). Given this, there is uncertainty about the effectiveness of exercise interventions on pain, as well as exercise interventions specifically for CANS pain. Variations in effectiveness may be due to many factors, including the exercise programme performed (i.e. aerobic or resistance training), the type of condition and underlying mechanisms causing the condition. It has also been proposed that exercise can improve function in people with pain, with strong evidence of a small effect ( Cohen 2021 ). Due to changes in pain and improvements in function, it is proposed that exercise for work‐related CANS can improve function, reduce absenteeism and enable return to work, allowing individuals to manage the day‐to‐day physical requirements of their work. Why it is important to do this review Work‐related complaints of the arm, neck or shoulder are common, have a large impact on many individuals and society, and frequently result in work loss ( HSE 2023 ; Kyung 2023 ; U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics 2023 ). Therefore, it is important to understand whether exercise interventions are effective in reducing pain and enhancing return to work. Further, an investigation of the effects of exercise is important to guide clinicians on the effectiveness of exercise for treating people with CANS. This ensures that people with CANS are provided the most effective and evidence‐based treatments. The most recent Cochrane review investigating conservative interventions (including exercise interventions) found very low‐quality evidence that exercise interventions did not improve pain, recovery, disability and sick leave in the short‐ or long‐term ( Verhagen 2013 ). Since then, several new studies on exercise interventions have been published. Therefore, it is important to determine if new evidence has an impact on previous results, and changes the final conclusion. We divided this review into two separate reviews ( Mehta 2022 and this current review), due to the size of the parent review ( Verhagen 2013 ). This review aims to answer the question: Do exercise interventions have a significant impact on short‐term and long‐term outcomes in adults with work‐related complaints of the arm, neck or shoulder? This review, which in part replaces Verhagen 2013 , provides an update of the evidence on this topic. Objectives To assess the effects of exercise interventions for work‐related complaints of the arm, neck or shoulder (CANS) in adults. The outcomes of interest are pain, function, work outcomes, adverse events, quality of life, healthcare use and injury recurrence. Methods Criteria for considering studies for this review Types of studies We will consider all randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi‐randomised controlled trials (using a method of allocating people to a treatment that is not strictly random, e.g. by date of birth, alternation). We will also consider cluster‐RCTs for inclusion, where randomisation is by groups of individuals, and cross‐over RCTs, in which the participants, upon completion of the course of one treatment, are switched to another. We will include studies published in full‐text articles, as abstracts only and unpublished data. Types of participants We will include studies that investigate adults (18 years and over) with work‐related CANS in any setting. We will consider complaints to be work‐related when this is stated in the text, or when people are selected from a specific working population, such as an office, factory, labourers, professional musicians, military personnel (without acute trauma), laboratory workers, healthcare workers and interns/apprentices. We will exclude studies where participants are diagnosed with acute trauma, neoplasm, inflammatory or neurological diseases. We will exclude professional athletes and university students from the included occupations. We will only include studies that include CANS and non‐CANS populations (i.e. work‐related complaints of other body areas, such as low back pain or studies with at‐risk populations), if the population with CANS is reported separately or the non‐CANS population represents less than 25% of the randomised participants. Types of interventions We will include trials studying exercise interventions for treating work‐related CANS. We define exercise as " ... participation in physical activity that is planned, structured, repetitive and purposeful for the improvement or maintenance of a specific health condition (or disease)" ( Nicolson 2017 , pp. 1). Examples of exercise interventions include regional stretching, strengthening and endurance exercises, general strengthening and aerobic training, postural correction exercises, and specific exercise therapies such as proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation (PNF), Mensendieck training or Feldenkrais therapy. We will include exercises of any schedule, dose, duration or intensity, so long as the exercise is performed on more than one session. Interventions can be applied in any setting, including work, home, rehabilitation clinics, specialised rehabilitation facilities or fitness centres. We will include exercise interventions that are delivered online or face‐to‐face, independent or supervised, and involve instructors qualified to supervise exercise programmes, including physiotherapists, occupational therapists, exercise physiologists, exercise scientists or fitness instructors. We will only include studies where participants have had at least one session with an instructor explaining the exercises. We will exclude exercise programmes where an exercise pamphlet is provided, but there are no sessions with an instructor. We will include combined interventions (i.e. exercise combined with ergonomics), so long as exercise constitutes at least 50% of the intervention. We will include studies with the following comparisons: exercise versus no intervention, minimal intervention or usual care; exercise plus co‐intervention versus co‐intervention alone (exercise as an add‐on treatment). We define the eligible comparator groups as follows: no intervention; 'wait and see': i.e. people in the control group are monitored but do not receive the intervention; waiting‐list control: people in the control group do not receive the intervention immediately but are on a waiting list to receive the intervention after completion of the study; minimal intervention: no more than one session of advice, discussion or counselling, or where participants are provided a pamphlet about an exercise programme without exercise‐related follow‐up; usual care: the control group does not receive additional care as a result of being in the trial or if 'usual care' fits the definition of 'no intervention' or 'minimal intervention'. Due to the inability to isolate the effects of exercise, we will exclude studies with the following comparisons: exercise versus active interventions (such as manual therapy, ultrasound, biopsychosocial rehabilitation programmes, relaxation, biofeedback, workplace modification or ergonomic intervention) or a combination of exercise and active interventions (i.e. in these, exercise is not an add‐on treatment); one exercise versus another exercise. Types of outcome measures We will include eligible studies regardless of whether they report the outcomes listed below. Primary outcomes Pain as a continuous outcome (lower values favour exercise); assessed, for example, with a visual analogue scale (0 to 10 or 0 to 100) ( Sriwatanakul 1983 ; Williamson 2005 ), a numerical rating scale (0 to 10 or 0 to 100) ( Williamson 2005 ), an ordinal scale ( Von Korff 2000 ), or the West Haven‐Yale Multidimensional Pain Inventory (WHYMPI) ( Kerns 1985 ). Functional status as a continuous outcome (higher values favour exercise); assessed, for example, with the Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand Measurement Tool (DASH) ( Hudak 1996 ), or the Health Assessment Questionnaire ( Fries 1982 ). Work‐related outcomes as continuous outcomes (lower values favour exercise); assessed, for example, with sickness absence (days off work), return to work (number of days), productivity loss at work (number of hours), or the Work Productivity and Activity Impairment Questionnaire ( Reilly 1993 ). Adverse events from the intervention as a dichotomous outcome (i.e. proportion with any adverse event, including falls or muscle tears). Secondary outcomes Quality of life as a continuous outcome; assessed, for example, with the 36‐item Short Form Survey ( Ware 1992 ), EQ‐5D‐5L ( Herdman 2011 ), the World Health Organization (WHO) Quality of Life (WHOQUAL‐BREF) instrument ( WHOQOL Group 1998 ), the WHOQOL tool ( WHOQOL Group 1995 ), or the Sickness Impact Profile ( De Bruin 1994 ). Healthcare consumption as a continuous outcome; assessed, for example, by the number of healthcare consultations, number of ergonomic adjustments, or amount of analgesic intake (mg/day). Recurrence of injury, disorder or complaint as a dichotomous outcome (e.g. per cent of individuals with the same injury within one year). We will consider two follow‐up time points: short‐term (≤ three months after randomisation) or long‐term (six months or longer after randomisation). If a study includes multiple follow‐up time points within the same category, we will select the time point that is closest to the completion of the intervention (for the short‐term time point), and closest to six months (for the long‐term follow‐up time point). We will prioritise the scales in the order specified above, in the case of multiple scales measuring an outcome domain. Search methods for identification of studies Electronic searches Verhagen 2013 was the last Cochrane review to cover this topic, with searches to 31 May 2013. As we have modified the inclusion and exclusion criteria, we will use the previously identified studies as one source and screen the other sources from inception, with the new criteria. We will search the following sources from inception to the date of search: Cochrane Central Register of Controlled trials (CENTRAL, from inception to current issue); MEDLINE (via Ovid, 1946 to present); Embase (via Ovid, 1974 to present); CINAHL (Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature; via EBSCOhost, 1981 to present); AMED (Allied and Complementary Medicine; Ovid, 1985 to present); PsycINFO (EBSCOhost, 1806 to present). We will separately search the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform ( trialsearch.who.int , to date of search) and ClinicalTrials.gov ( clinicaltrials.gov , to the date of search) for any unpublished and ongoing studies. We will apply no language restrictions. We will use a subject‐specific strategy including title, abstract, keywords and medical subject heading (MeSH) terms, where relevant. We will combine the subject‐specific search with the sensitivity‐ and precision‐maximising version of the Cochrane Highly Sensitive Search Strategy for identifying randomised trials in MEDLINE and modified for use in other databases ( Lefebvre 2022 ). Search strategies for all databases are shown in Appendix 1 . Searching other resources We will also search the reference lists of included articles and contact experts in the field. Data collection and analysis Selection of studies Two review authors (from PWS, PM, SJT and JT) will independently select trials by inspecting titles, keywords and abstracts to determine if the studies meet the inclusion criteria for design, participants and intervention. We will retrieve full publications of possibly relevant studies for final assessment. Next, review authors will independently select the trials to be included. We will resolve disagreements by consensus and, if necessary, by third party adjudication (APV). We will contact study authors for missing information that will help determine eligibility. We will classify studies as 'awaiting assessment' if there is insufficient information to determine eligibility. We will record excluded studies at this stage, or subsequent stages, in a ‘characteristics of excluded studies’ table, with a reason for exclusion. We will collate multiple reports of the same study, so that each study, rather than each report, is the unit of interest in the review. We will record the selection process in sufficient detail to complete a PRISMA flow diagram ( Page 2021 ). Data extraction and management Two review authors (from PWS, PM, SJT and JT) will independently extract the following study data. Trial characteristics, including design (parallel, cross‐over, cluster), number of people randomised, country of participant recruitment, sources of funding and declared conflicts of interest. Participant characteristics, including diagnosis, age, sex, ethnicity/race and duration of symptoms. Intervention characteristics, including setting of intervention (i.e. home, work, fitness centre), type of exercise (i.e. strength, aerobic, stretching, motor control, PNF, Mensendieck training, Feldenkrais therapy or mixed therapy (with exercise type indicated)), instructor qualification, number of supervised and unsupervised sessions and mode of supervision (face‐to‐face or online), exercise schedule, length of intervention (weeks), time per exercise session, sessions per week, total number of sessions and if the exercise programme was progressive (i.e. increased difficulty through the sessions). We will extract details of the comparator intervention, including the type of comparator (e.g. no intervention, minimal intervention) and details of the comparator if a minimal intervention has been used. We will follow the recommendations of the template for intervention description and replication (TIDieR) to extract intervention‐related data ( Hoffmann 2014 ). Outcomes reported, including the outcome measurement, direction of the measure (e.g. if higher values favour exercise), means and standard deviations for continuous variables (pain, function and quality of life), the number of events reported for dichotomous variables (such as adverse events or recurrence of injury). These data will be extracted as detailed in Types of outcome measures . We will extract outcomes for each follow‐up period. Risk of bias will be extracted as detailed in Assessment of risk of bias in included studies . We will resolve any disagreements by consensus and, if necessary, by third party adjudication (APV). We will pilot the Excel form prior to data extraction for the review. Assessment of risk of bias in included studies Two review authors (from PWS, PM, SJT and JT) will independently assess risk of bias using version 2 of the Cochrane risk of bias tool (RoB 2) for randomised trials ( Sterne 2019 ), and will consult a third author (APV) in case of disagreements. We will assess studies according to the recommendations in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions ( Higgins 2022 ) . We will reassess studies from the Verhagen 2013 version of the review using RoB 2. We will evaluate cluster‐RCTs for risk of bias using the extension of the RoB 2 tool, which includes additional domains for identification/recruitment bias ( Eldridge 2021 ). We will assess cross‐over trials using the supplement to RoB 2, accounting for the cross‐over design ( Higgins 2021 ). We will use Review Manager software to generate figures showing our assessment of the risk of bias ( RevMan 2022 ). We will evaluate the risk of bias of the following main outcomes at the time point closest to the completion of the intervention (short‐term time point): pain; functional status; work‐related outcomes; adverse events from intervention. For this review, we will assess the 'intention‐to‐treat effect' (i.e. the effect of the assignment to the intervention at baseline). We will rate each study as having a high risk of bias, raising 'some concerns' for risk of bias, or having a low risk of bias, according to the following domains ( Sterne 2019 ; Higgins 2022 ): bias arising from the randomisation process; bias due to deviations from intended interventions; bias due to missing outcome data; bias in measurement of the outcome; and bias in selection of the reported result. We will use signalling questions for each domain via an Excel spreadsheet, which provides an algorithm to calculate domain bias. Overall, domain level bias will be classified as ‘low risk of bias’, ‘some concerns’, or ‘high risk of bias’. We will determine the overall risk of bias as 'low risk' when all domains are judged as low risk of bias. We will define a study as having ‘some concerns’ for risk of bias if the study is judged to raise some concerns in at least one domain, but not to be at high risk of bias for any domain. We will define a study to have an overall 'high risk of bias' when at least one domain is 'high risk' or when the study is judged to have 'some concerns' for multiple domains, in a way that substantially lowers confidence in the result. We will make the grading Excel spreadsheet available through an online server. Measures of treatment effect We will present the various outcome measures separately. For dichotomous data, we will express the results, where possible, as risk ratios (RR) or risk differences (RD) with corresponding 95% confidence intervals. We will calculate mean differences (MD) or, where outcome measurement instruments are dissimilar, standardised mean differences (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals for continuous data ( Lau 1997 ). Unit of analysis issues For studies with multiple trial arms, we will combine groups to make a single pairwise comparison so long as the groups are similar enough to combine. If we determine that the groups are too different to combine, we will select the most relevant pair of interventions and exclude the others. For cluster‐randomised trials that do not adjust for a cluster effect, we will adjust the sample sizes using an intracluster coefficient estimate from the trial or another source. If this is not possible, we will conduct a sensitivity analysis that excludes cluster‐randomised trials. For cross‐over trials, we will only use data from the first phase, unless a carryover effect is unlikely. We will exclude cross‐over trials from the analysis if we cannot use the data from the first phase and a carryover effect is likely. We acknowledge that this approach will result in a biased and conservative estimate of the effect size. Dealing with missing data We will contact trial authors to request any missing data. Where possible, we will perform intention‐to‐treat analyses to include all people randomised with follow‐up data (where applicable). For dichotomous and continuous data, if we identify dropouts, we will use the actual number of participants contributing data at the relevant outcome assessment. We will impute standard deviation values from baseline standard deviations or the standard deviations of a similar study, when confidence intervals or standard errors of the same study are unavailable. We will perform sensitivity analyses to assess studies where assumptions about data are made. We will address the potential impact of missing data on the findings of the review in the Discussion section. Assessment of heterogeneity The clinician in the review team (SS) will assess clinical heterogeneity using information about the study population, exercise intervention, control interventions and outcomes. We will assess statistical heterogeneity between pooled trials considering the Chi 2 test and I 2 statistic ( Deeks 2022 ). If heterogeneity is identified, we will explore the options outlined in the Cochrane Handbook ( Deeks 2022 ), and investigate outlier studies. If we cannot explain the heterogeneity, we will downgrade the certainty of the evidence. In addition, we will calculate prediction intervals (using causal mediation analysis (CMA) prediction intervals) to estimate the variability of the true effect size across studies. Assessment of reporting biases We will assess publication bias using a funnel plot and Eggers' statistic if there are at least 10 studies included in the meta‐analysis ( Eggers 1997 ). Data synthesis We will use Review Manager (RevMan) to analyse the data ( RevMan 2022 ). We will include all eligible studies in the analysis. In the previous review ( Verhagen 2013 ), we pooled studies that we judged to be clinically similar regarding participants, interventions, comparisons and outcomes. Should pooling be possible again with new trials included, we will pool results of comparable groups of trials using a random‐effects model and 95% confidence intervals. We will use a random‐effects model because of the likely clinical heterogeneity between populations and interventions included in the review. For studies that cannot be pooled in a meta‐analysis, we will follow the methods described in the Synthesis Without Meta‐analysis (SWiM) reporting guideline ( Campbell 2020 ). Subgroup analysis and investigation of heterogeneity If sufficient data are available, we will perform subgroup analyses to evaluate the effects of: location of the complaint (neck/shoulder versus arm), as the location of the complaint can affect recovery ( Cohen 2021 ); type of work (office work versus manual work) as the types of injuries sustained may be different due to the physicality of the work and the mechanism of injury; duration of the complaint ((sub)acute (≤ three months) versus chronic (> three months)), as prognoses are different for people with acute and chronic pain ( Cohen 2021 ). We will compare subgroups using the formal test for subgroups in RevMan ( RevMan 2022 ). We will assess the proportion of total variability due to between‐study heterogeneity using the I 2 statistic in RevMan ( RevMan 2022 ). We will use the following thresholds for interpretation, as well as the magnitude and direction of the effects and the strength of the evidence for the proportion of total variability due to between‐study heterogeneity ( Deeks 2022 ). We will interpret I 2 values as follows: 0% to 40%: might not be important; 30% to 60%: may represent moderate heterogeneity; 50% to 90%: may represent substantial heterogeneity; 75% to 100%: considerable heterogeneity. Sensitivity analysis We will perform sensitivity analyses relating to the study methodology, such as studies that have low risk of bias and 'some concerns' for bias, removing studies that require data assumptions, pooling studies that have adequate randomisation, removing cluster‐randomised trials and evaluating the effects of studies with complete data. Summary of findings and assessment of the certainty of the evidence We will create two summary of findings tables: (1) exercise versus no intervention, minimal intervention or usual care and (2) exercise plus co‐intervention versus co‐intervention alone. Two independent review authors (from PWS, PM, SJT and JT) will create the summary of findings tables, with disagreements being resolved by a third author (APV). We will provide a summary of findings for the following main outcomes at the time point closest to the completion of the intervention (short‐term time point): pain: continuous outcome, with mixed outcome measures (e.g. visual analogue scale, numerical rating scale); functional status: continuous outcome, with mixed outcome measures (e.g. Health Assessment Questionnaire, DASH)); work‐related outcomes: continuous outcomes, with mixed outcome measures (e.g. sickness absence (days), return to work (days)); adverse events from intervention: dichotomous outcome (yes/no). We will include the following information in the summary of findings tables: population, intervention, comparator, outcomes (listed above) and time point of assessment; illustrative comparative risks; absolute and relative effect magnitudes; total participants and number of studies; certainty of the evidence using GRADE; comments and footnotes spelling out abbreviations and providing additional information to aid readers' interpretation of the table. We will assess the overall certainty of evidence and strength of the recommendation using GRADE, as recommended in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions ( Schünemann 2022 ), using GRADEpro GDT software ( GRADEpro GDT ). We will downgrade the certainty of the evidence for a specific outcome for limitations in each of the following domains ( Schünemann 2022 ). Limitations in design. If more than 25% of the participants come from studies with an overall high risk of bias, we will downgrade by one level; if more than 50% of the participants come from studies with an overall high risk of bias, we will downgrade by two levels. Inconsistency of results (statistical heterogeneity). If the I 2 statistic is greater than 40%, we will downgrade by one level; if I 2 is greater than 75%, we will downgrade by two levels. We will downgrade by one level for inconsistent findings amongst studies (≤ 75% of participants reported findings in the same direction). Indirectness (i.e. generalisability of the findings). If more than 50% of the participants are outside the target group, we will downgrade by one level. We will not downgrade this item by more than one level. Imprecision. We will downgrade by one level if there are fewer than 300 participants for dichotomous outcomes and fewer than 400 participants for continuous outcomes. Other (e.g. publication bias and flawed designs). We will justify all decisions to downgrade the certainty of evidence and report these to readers to aid understanding of the reasons. Two review authors will independently rate the level of evidence for each outcome using these five domains, and resolve any disagreements by consulting a third review author. We will apply the following categories to describe the certainty of the evidence: high certainty: further research is very unlikely to change the level of confidence; all domains are fulfilled; moderate certainty: further research is likely to have an important impact on the confidence in the estimate of effects and may change the estimate; one domain is not fulfilled; low certainty: further research is very likely to have an important impact on our confidence in the estimate of effects and is likely to change it; two of the domains are not fulfilled; very low certainty: large uncertainty about the estimate; three of the domains are not fulfilled. Single studies of fewer than 300 participants (for dichotomous outcomes) or fewer than 400 participants (for continuous outcomes) will start at low‐certainty evidence, as we determine these to be inconsistent and imprecise. This could be further downgraded to very low‐certainty evidence if there are also limitations in design, indirectness or other considerations. We will include studies judged to be at an overall high risk of bias, some concerns and low risk of bias in the primary GRADE analysis. We will use the methods and recommendations described in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions ( Higgins 2021 ), using GRADEpro software. We will justify all decisions to downgrade the certainty of the body of evidence using footnotes. We will conduct the review according to this published protocol, and report any deviations from it in the review's 'Differences between protocol and review' section. documents.title: Stem cell injections for osteoarthritis of the knee.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Stem cells are specialised precursor cells that can replace aged or damaged cells and thereby maintain healthy tissue function. Stem cell therapy is increasingly used as a treatment for knee osteoarthritis, despite the lack of clarity around the mechanism by which stem cell therapy may slow down disease progression in osteoarthritis, and uncertainty regarding its benefits and harms.
OBJECTIVES: To assess the benefits and harms of stem cell injections for people with osteoarthritis of the knee. A secondary objective is to maintain the currency of the evidence, using a living systematic review approach.
SEARCH METHODS: We searched the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE and Embase on 15 September 2023, unrestricted by date or language of publication. We also searched ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) for relevant trial protocols and ongoing trials.
SELECTION CRITERIA: We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs), or trials using quasi-randomised methods of participant allocation, comparing stem cell injection with placebo injection, no treatment or usual care, glucocorticoid injection, other injections, exercise, drug therapy, surgical interventions, and supplements and complementary therapies in people with knee osteoarthritis.
DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS: Two review authors selected studies for inclusion, extracted trial characteristics and outcome data, assessed risk of bias and assessed the certainty of evidence using the GRADE approach. The primary comparison was stem cell injection compared with placebo injection. The primary time point for pain, function and quality of life was three to six months, and the end of the trial period for participant-reported success, joint structure changes and adverse event outcomes. Major outcomes were pain, function, quality of life, global assessment of success, radiographic joint progression, withdrawals due to adverse events and serious adverse events.
MAIN RESULTS: We found 25 randomised trials (1341 participants) comparing stem cell injections with placebo injection (eight trials), no treatment or usual care (analgesia, weight loss and exercise) (two trials), glucocorticoid injection (one trial), hyaluronic acid injection (seven trials), platelet-rich plasma injections (two trials), oral acetaminophen (paracetamol) (one trial), non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs plus physical therapy plus hyaluronic acid injection (one trial) and stem cell injection plus intra-articular co-intervention versus co-intervention alone (three trials) in people with osteoarthritis of the knee. Trials were predominantly small, with sample sizes ranging from 6 to 252 participants, with only two trials having more than 100 participants. The average age of participants across trials ranged from 51 to 66 years, and symptom duration varied from one to 10 years. Placebo-controlled trials were largely free from bias, while most trials without a placebo control were susceptible to performance and detection biases. Here, we limit reporting to the main comparison, stem cell injection versus placebo injection. Compared with placebo injection, stem cell injection may slightly improve pain and function up to six months after treatment. Mean pain (0 to 10 scale, 0 no pain) was 4.5 out of 10 points with placebo injection and 1.2 points better (2.5 points better to 0 points better) with stem cell injection (I2 = 80%; 7 studies, 445 participants). Mean function (0 to 100 scale, 0 best function) was 46.3 points with placebo injection and 14.2 points better (25.3 points better to 3.1 points better) with stem cell injection (I2 = 82%; 7 studies, 432 participants). We are uncertain whether stem cell injections improve quality of life or increase the number of people who report treatment success compared to placebo injection, because the certainty of the evidence was very low. Mean quality of life was 45.3 points with placebo injection and 22.8 points better (18.0 points worse to 63.7 points better) with stem cell injection (I2 = 96%; 2 studies, 288 participants) at up to six months follow-up. At the end of follow-up, 89/168 participants (530 per 1000) in the placebo injection group reported treatment success compared with 126/180 participants (683 per 1000) in the stem cell injection group (risk ratio (RR) 1.29, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.53; I2 = 0%; 4 trials, 348 participants). We downgraded the evidence to low certainty for pain and function due to indirectness (as the source, method of preparation and dose of stem cells varied across studies), and suspected publication bias (up to three larger RCTs have been conducted but withdrawn prior to reporting of results). For quality of life and treatment success, we further downgraded the evidence to very low certainty due to imprecision in addition to indirectness and suspected publication bias. We are uncertain of the potential harms associated with stem cell injection, as there were very low event rates for serious adverse events. At the end of follow-up, 5/219 participants (23 per 1000) in the placebo injection group experienced serious adverse events compared with 4/242 participants (16 per 1000) in the stem cell injection group (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.20 to 2.64; I2 = 0%; 7 trials, 461 participants) and there were no reported withdrawals due to adverse events. We downgraded the evidence to very low certainty due to indirectness, suspected publication bias and imprecision. Radiographic progression was not assessed in any of the included studies.
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: Compared with placebo injections and based upon low-certainty evidence, stem cell injections for people with knee osteoarthritis may slightly improve pain and function. We are uncertain of the effects of stem cell injections on quality of life or the number who report treatment success. Although the putative benefits of stem cell therapies for osteoarthritis include potential regenerative effects on damaged tissues, particularly articular cartilage, we remain uncertain of the effect of stem cell injections on structural progression in the knee (measured by radiographic appearance). There is also uncertainty regarding the safety of stem cell injections. Serious adverse events were infrequently reported, although all invasive joint procedures (including injections) carry a small risk of septic arthritis. The risk of other important harms, including potential concerns related to the use of a therapy with the theoretical capacity to promote cell growth, or to the use of allogeneic cells, remains unknown.

documents.title: Effectiveness of isometric exercise in the management of tendinopathy: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials.
documents.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To systematically review and critically appraise the literature on the effectiveness of isometric exercise in comparison with other treatment strategies or no treatment in tendinopathy.
DESIGN: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
DATA SOURCES: Electronic searches of Medline, Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature, EMBASE and Cochrane were undertaken from inception to May 2020.
METHODS: Overall quality of each study was determined based on a combined assessment of internal validity, external validity and precision. For each outcome measure, level of evidence was rated based on the system by van Tulder et al.
RESULTS: Ten studies were identified and included in the review, including participants with patellar (n=4), rotator cuff (n=2), lateral elbow (n=2), Achilles (n=1) and gluteal (n=1) tendinopathies. Three were of good and seven were of poor overall quality. Based on limited evidence (level 3), isometric exercise was not superior to isotonic exercise for chronic tendinopathy either immediately following treatment or in the short term (≤12 weeks) for any of the investigated outcome measures. Additionally, for acute rotator cuff tendinopathy, isometric exercise appears to be no more effective than ice therapy in the short term (limited evidence; level 3).
SUMMARY: Isometric exercise does not appear to be superior to isotonic exercise in the management of chronic tendinopathy. The response to isometric exercise is variable both within and across tendinopathy populations. Isometric exercise can be used as part of a progressive loading programme as it may be beneficial for selected individuals.
PROSPERO REGISTRATION NUMBER: CRD42019147179.

Abstract Objective To systematically review and critically appraise the literature on the effectiveness of isometric exercise in comparison with other treatment strategies or no treatment in tendinopathy. Design A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. Data sources Electronic searches of Medline, Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature, EMBASE and Cochrane were undertaken from inception to May 2020. Methods Overall quality of each study was determined based on a combined assessment of internal validity, external validity and precision. For each outcome measure, level of evidence was rated based on the system by van Tulder et al . Results Ten studies were identified and included in the review, including participants with patellar (n=4), rotator cuff (n=2), lateral elbow (n=2), Achilles (n=1) and gluteal (n=1) tendinopathies. Three were of good and seven were of poor overall quality. Based on limited evidence (level 3), isometric exercise was not superior to isotonic exercise for chronic tendinopathy either immediately following treatment or in the short term (≤12 weeks) for any of the investigated outcome measures. Additionally, for acute rotator cuff tendinopathy, isometric exercise appears to be no more effective than ice therapy in the short term (limited evidence; level 3).
