Discussion This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy of MRT in patients with NSSP across seven randomized controlled trials involving 244 patients. The quality of the included studies was rated moderate to good. Despite the limited number of studies, the findings indicate that MRT techniques are statistically more effective than conventional physiotherapy in reducing pain intensity (moderate certainty), improving range of motion (mostly moderate certainty), enhancing functional outcomes (moderate-to-high certainty), and decreasing pain-related fear (high certainty). This meta-analysis identified a significant difference in pain intensity with MRT in patients with NSSP, characterized by a high effect size and high heterogeneity. In contrast, two studies—Walankar & Shah (2023) (action observation therapy) 47 and Hekim et al. 33 (Mirror therapy)—found no significant difference in pain reduction between MRT and control groups. Across all included studies, both intervention and control groups achieved a 2 cm reduction on the Visual Analog Scale (VAS), which is considered the minimal clinically important difference according to Portney and Watkins 48 , except for the control group in the study by Grudut et al., 2022 42 . This indicates that while control groups, including those receiving traditional physiotherapy, also achieved clinical significance in terms of pain reduction, MRT groups are more effective in reducing pain intensity (moderate certainty). Indeed, in an umbrella and mapping review with meta-meta-analysis study by Cuenca-Martínez et al. (2021), similar to our meta-analysis results, MRT techniques were found to reduce chronic musculoskeletal pain. However, the results emphasized by our study do not include conditions such as neuropathic pain or phantom pain and post-stroke pain 49 . The basic mechanism by which MRT produces hypoalgesia in patients with musculoskeletal pain 17 is thought to be due to the inputs generated by the techniques reorganizing cortical processes in the primary somatosensory cortex that are disrupted by pain 50 , 51 . It has been reported that the mirror neuron system, which provides neuroanatomical support, is extensively involved in the motor learning process through movement representation 52 , 53 . Furthermore, the effects related to the representation of movement in the brain indicate that cortico-subcortical networks involved in planning, execution, adjustment, and automatization of actual movements share similar neurophysiological activity. It has been shown that this neurophysiological activity can be influenced by specific physical, cognitive-evaluative, motivational-emotional and direct modulation variables related to the movement representation process 54 . MRT has also been shown to have an effect on a number of intriguing variables, such as strength 17 , 54 , 55 and lead to the improvement of motor learning processes 56 , 57 . The present meta-analysis supports the aforementioned mechanisms by demonstrating that MRT produces a significant difference in functionality and range of motion measurements (except for internal rotation) with a moderate effect size in patients with NSSP. Similar to the pain analysis, the mirror therapy groups in the studies by Walankar and Shah 47 and Hekim et al. 33 did not show statistically significant improvement in functionality (moderate-to-high certainty) compared to the control group. In addition, all intervention and control groups in the included studies achieved minimal clinical differences for measures of functionality 58 . The presence of pain-induced avoidance and fear of movement has been noted in various musculoskeletal pain conditions, not limited to shoulder pain 59 – 62 . Furthermore, a negative correlation has been identified between kinesiophobia levels and the ability to form both kinesthetic and visual motor images in patients with chronic low back pain 63 . Additionally, it has been observed that patients with chronic low back pain exhibit impaired motor image formation abilities compared to healthy individuals 63 , 64 . Therefore, it can be hypothesized that MRT, which enhances the capacity to form visual motor images, may positively impact fear of pain. Indeed, the current meta-analysis of four studies 42 , 45 – 47 on fear of pain (high certainty) demonstrates that MRT was highly effective. Limitations of the study and suggestions for future studies Although the current meta-analysis is the first to demonstrate the effect of MRT in patients with NSSP, the study has several limitations. These include the relatively high heterogeneity among the included studies, the small number of patients, variations in the timing of measurements across studies (ranging from 3 weeks to 10 weeks), and the absence of evaluation of long-term outcomes. In this meta-analysis, no publication bias was detected, and adjustments according to Duval and Tweedie’s calculations had minimal impact on the effect size values. However, the limited number of published studies increases the likelihood of publication bias. Therefore, future randomized controlled trials addressing these limitations are warranted. In the studies included in the meta-analysis, blinding of the physiotherapist and patients could not be ensured and this constitutes one of the main limitations of the study by creating a risk of bias. Blinding was mostly based on assessor blinding. Despite this, most of the results were based on self-reported measures, which also prevented blinding of the assessors. Although blinding of participants and therapists in an exercise trial is challenging to achieve and cannot eliminate the risk of bias, future studies should at least attempt to limit potential bias through appropriate blinding of assessors. This is because certain expectations and beliefs of patients and therapists may influence the results. Furthermore, in all studies, the control group and the intervention group consisted of different groups, and there was no crossover experimental design in the studies. Consequently, the outcomes of the included studies are likely to be affected by discrepancies in exercise intensity and blinding procedure between the groups. In all studies included in the meta-analysis, conventional physiotherapy methods included electrotherapy, range of motion exercises, stretching techniques, while in some studies mobilization 46 , 47 and some simple strengthening exercises 45 – 47 were added to these techniques. Differences between the rehabilitation of these control groups may also affect the results of the study. In addition, due to the small number of studies, all MRT techniques were included in the meta-analysis process as if they were a single technique. This constitutes one of the main limitations of the meta-analysis. Because it is concluded that the mirror neuron system works more efficiently through action observation therapy than motor imagery and action observation therapy is less demanding in terms of cognitive load than motor imagery. There is also evidence that action observation therapy may be less sensitive to the influence of variables related to motion representation 54 . Similarly, it has been suggested that the neuronal mechanisms behind mirror therapy and motor imagery are different 65 . The brain’s natural tendency to prioritize visual feedback over others is thought to make mirror therapy a more powerful tool. However, research evidence to support this hypothesis is currently lacking 66 , 67 . It is possible that there may also be differences between the visual mirror feedback group and the mirror therapy group. In fact, some studies in healthy individuals have shown that appropriate feedback can affect motor recovery and improve motor performance in the short or long term 33 , 68 – 71 . Specifically, in the Hekim et al. study included in the meta-analysis, visual mirror therapy was found to be superior to mirror therapy. Because graded motor imagery is a therapy that uses right-left discrimination, motor imagery, and mirror therapy in a particular way, its mechanism has not been fully explored 72 . Therefore, more studies comparing MRT methods and investigating mechanisms in patients with NSSP are needed in the future. In summary, the relatively small sample sizes and heterogeneity in study designs and intervention protocols in the studies included in this meta-analysis may have influenced the results. Future research should aim to address these limitations by conducting larger, well-powered, and rigorously designed randomized controlled trials. Additionally, future studies could employ neuroimaging techniques to elucidate the neural correlates of MRT and identify potential biomarkers for treatment response. Examining the long-term effects of MRT on pain, function, and quality of life in patients with NSSP is also crucial. Although this meta-analysis focused on short-term outcomes, it is important to evaluate whether the benefits of MRT persist over time. Lastly, future research should investigate the optimal dosage and frequency of MRT sessions to maximize therapeutic benefits. Exploring the potential combination of MRT with other interventions, such as cognitive-behavioral therapy or exercise therapy, may also yield synergistic effects. Conclusion In conclusion, although caution is warranted when interpreting these findings due to the limited number of studies included in the current meta-analysis, it was determined that MRT techniques had a positive effect on pain, range of motion, functional outcomes, and pain-related fear in NSSP patients. Given the limitations of the current studies, there is a need for further planned studies. Electronic supplementary material Below is the link to the electronic supplementary material. documents.title: A systematic review of the biomechanical and biological impacts of ultrasound waves on skeletal tissues.
documents.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Ultrasound waves can affect bone and bone marrow, and widespread medical and industrial use increases the likelihood of direct or indirect exposure. This systematic review summarizes current evidence on the biological and biomechanical effects of high- and low-intensity ultrasound on skeletal tissues, with emphasis on safety.
METHODS: A systematic search was conducted across PubMed, ScienceDirect, Wiley Online Library, EMBASE, JSTOR, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, and Google Scholar (up to October 2024), guided by a PICO-based strategy. Studies were screened using predefined eligibility criteria, and 29 articles met the inclusion criteria for synthesis. Study quality was appraised using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) and the 2018 Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD42024620731).
RESULTS: Ultrasound technology has significant implications for health and safety due to its medical and industrial applications. High-intensity ultrasound waves may cause tissue damage, reduce bone density, and even lead to necrosis. However, controlled low-intensity ultrasound can be beneficial in medical treatments and tissue healing.
CONCLUSIONS: To minimize potential risks, it is crucial to establish safety standards and enhance public awareness regarding the appropriate use of ultrasound technology. In summary, while prolonged exposure to ultrasound may adversely affect bone density and marrow integrity, the technology retains significant value in diagnostic and therapeutic applications.
documents.conclusions: To minimize potential risks, it is crucial to establish safety standards and enhance public awareness regarding the appropriate use of ultrasound technology. In summary, while prolonged exposure to ultrasound may adversely affect bone density and marrow integrity, the technology retains significant value in diagnostic and therapeutic applications.

The frequency of ultrasound typically ranges from 20 kHz to several gigahertz (GHz). Frequencies above 20 kHz are classified as ultrasonic and are used in fields such as medical imaging and industrial applications. The common frequencies for diagnostic ultrasound typically range between 2 and 18 MHz [ 2 ]. The term ‘ultrasonic’ refers to devices and technologies that utilize these frequencies for specific purposes, such as medical imaging or defect detection in materials. In contrast, ‘ultrasound’ refers to the high-frequency sound waves themselves, which have significant effects on human health [ 3 , 4 ], particularly in relation to bone and bone marrow. These waves are increasingly produced by high-power medical devices and industrial applications, raising concerns about potential risks associated with exposure [ 5 ]. Ultrasound is not limited to conventional Brightness mode imaging (B-mode) and has expanded into several specialized applications that provide functional and quantitative information. Doppler ultrasound enables assessment of vascular hemodynamics and blood-flow changes and has been applied, for example, in evaluating carotid artery flow alterations in clinical risk settings [ 6 ]. In addition, ultrasound elastography has gained substantial attention as a non-invasive approach for characterizing tissue mechanical properties by providing qualitative and quantitative measures of stiffness, while also presenting modality-specific limitations that should be considered in clinical interpretation [ 7 ]. Ultrasound has also been used in dosimetry-related research; for instance, acoustic parameters such as sound speed and attenuation have been investigated as quantitative indicators in polymer gel dosimeters for monitoring radiation dose-dependent changes [ 8 ]. Together, these applications highlight the versatility of ultrasound across diagnostic assessment, tissue characterization, and quantitative measurement frameworks. On the other hand, high-intensity ultrasound can cause damage to soft and bone tissues. This type of ultrasound, due to excessive heat generation and pressure, can lead to necrosis (cell death) and tissue damage. Moreover, in specific conditions or disease stages, such as the presence of tumors, ultrasound exposure may stimulate tumor growth. On the other hand, low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS), which typically operates at intensities below 100 mW/cm 2 , often around 20–50 mW/cm 2 , has been found to enhance bone differentiation, stimulate cell proliferation, and promote angiogenesis [ 9 ]. LIPUS also increases the expression of bone markers and calcium deposition, aiding in fracture healing and bone tissue integration. Conversely, high-intensity ultrasound can reduce bone growth and cause tissue damage, especially if the transducer remains fixed in one position. Ultrasound has long been utilized for therapeutic purposes in medicine and has proven beneficial in various applications. Low-power ultrasound, particularly at frequencies around 1 MHz, has been widely used since the 1950s in physiotherapy to treat conditions such as tendinitis and bursitis. In the 1980s, high-pressure shock waves were introduced for kidney stone treatment, leading to the development of lithotripsy, which quickly replaced surgery as the primary treatment option [ 10 ]. Prolonged or repeated exposure to ultrasonic waves may have adverse effects. The potential for biological effects of ultrasound was first reported in 1917 when Langevin demonstrated that fish in a small tank died when exposed to ultrasonic waves [ 11 ]. Negative effects include functional changes in cardiovascular and nervous systems, cavitation, necrosis (cell death), damage to bone tissues, bleeding near bone regions, increased apoptosis (programmed cell death) in tissues adjacent to bone, and adverse effects on bone marrow function. Additionally, improper use of ultrasound devices may lead to localized infections, thermal injuries, and metabolic changes. Therefore, precise regulation and further research are necessary to fully understand the impact of ultrasound exposure on human health, particularly for workers in environments with high levels of ultrasonic noise [ 12 – 15 ]. Furthermore, some studies suggest that ultrasound waves may negatively impact bone marrow cells by reducing their ability to produce blood cells. Hence, comprehensive research is needed to assess the occupational risks of exposure to these waves. Protection from inappropriate or hazardous ultrasonic exposure is governed by international standards and national regulations. IEC 60601, Part 1, specifies mechanical, electrical, chemical, and thermal safety requirements for electromechanical medical devices. In Part 2 of this standard, no upper limit is set for ultrasonic exposure in diagnostic ultrasound equipment; instead, safety indices are defined to guide users on thermal and mechanical risks [ 16 ]. Therapeutic ultrasound is classified into two main types. The first type, high-intensity ultrasound, typically operates at frequencies above 1 MHz and intensities exceeding 1 W/cm 2 . This type of ultrasound can damage bone tissues by generating excessive heat and altering tissue structure. The second type, therapeutic ultrasound, operates at lower frequencies (1–3 MHz) and lower intensities, usually below 1 W/cm 2 [ 17 , 18 ]. This type of ultrasound can aid tissue repair, accelerate healing, and alleviate pain. Low-intensity ultrasound promotes the healing process and reduces inflammation. Thus, while high-intensity ultrasound may be harmful, low-intensity ultrasound is beneficial for treatment and recovery [ 19 ]. In this regard, ultrasound may influence the nourishment of several tissues, including bone and bone marrow. Before ultrasound-based treatments, patients should receive medical consultation and appropriate evaluation. Despite advances in ultrasound applications, important gaps remain in safety standards for this frequency range. Further studies are needed to better understand the biological effects of these waves [ 5 ]. Raising public awareness about the positive effects of ultrasound on bone health and methods for preventing potential damage can help protect workers and improve the quality of life for individuals exposed to these waves. Therefore, education and awareness about the safe and effective use of ultrasound in medical and industrial applications are crucial. These measures can reduce risks and enhance the efficiency of this technology. Despite the broad use of ultrasound and the growing literature on both therapeutic benefits and potential hazards, evidence related to skeletal tissues is dispersed across clinical, preclinical, and occupational research, and findings are not always consistent across exposure types and outcome measures. Therefore, the aim of this systematic review is to synthesize and critically evaluate the available evidence on the biomechanical and biological effects of ultrasound exposure across low- and high-intensity modalities on bone and bone marrow structure and function, with particular attention to safety implications in both clinical and occupational settings. Materials and methods This systematic review examines the effects of low- and high-intensity ultrasound waves on bone and bone marrow tissues, with a focus on their physiological and biological impacts. To achieve a comprehensive understanding of the subject, an extensive literature search was conducted across PubMed, ScienceDirect, Wiley Online Library, CIVILICA, EMBASE, JSTOR, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, and Google Scholar, covering studies published between 1990 and 2024 (Table 1 ). The search strategy was designed using Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) keywords, including “Ultrasound waves (High-Intensity and Low-Intensity), Bone, Bone Marrow, and Systematic Review.” The retrieved articles encompassed original research, review papers, experimental studies, and clinical reports from various disciplines, including medical imaging, physiotherapy, occupational health, and biomedical engineering. The initial database search yielded 76,983 records. After removing irrelevant articles and those not meeting the input criteria, 403 studies remained for preliminary evaluation. Duplicate entries ( n = 30) were then removed, leaving 381 articles for title and abstract screening. At this stage, 352 records were excluded due to lack of relevance or insufficient data, resulting in 29 articles that met all eligibility criteria and were included in the final synthesis (Fig. 1 ). Exclusion criteria included studies that: Focused on non-skeletal tissues or solely on device mechanics; Lacked experimental or clinical relevance; or Provided insufficient methodological details for quality appraisal. This rigorous screening process ensured that the selected literature provided high-quality evidence regarding the physiological responses of bone and bone marrow to ultrasound exposure, both in therapeutic and occupational contexts (details are provided in “ Appendix ”). Additional methodological details include a comprehensive risk of bias assessment and a focused PICO analysis. Results This study analyzed the physical effects of ultrasound exposure in both industrial and medical settings by reviewing 29 research articles. The findings highlight the diverse impacts of ultrasound waves on bone tissue and bone marrow, emphasizing the influence of various factors, such as frequency, intensity, and duration of exposure. The key outcomes of the review suggest that while ultrasound has significant therapeutic potential, improper exposure parameters may lead to adverse effects on bone integrity. The reviewed studies indicate that LIPUS can enhance bone regeneration, accelerate fracture healing, and promote osteogenic differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells. Conversely, high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) has been associated with localized thermal damage, osteocyte necrosis, and potential weakening of bone structure, especially at frequencies exceeding safe exposure limits. Table 4 provides a comprehensive summary of the reviewed studies, detailing the authors, publication years, experimental methodologies, key results, and factors influencing ultrasound effects on bone and bone marrow. This table serves as a valuable reference for researchers, clinicians, and industrial professionals by enabling easy access to critical data for comparative analysis and decision-making. The inclusion of various research methodologies allows for a deeper understanding of the different scientific approaches used in ultrasound studies. The review underscores the importance of optimizing ultrasound parameters to maximize therapeutic benefits while minimizing potential risks. A careful selection of ultrasound type, exposure duration, and intensity is essential to achieving the desired biological effects while reducing the likelihood of adverse outcomes. The study also emphasizes the need for further research to better understand the underlying biomechanical and physiological mechanisms influenced by ultrasound waves. From a practical perspective, these findings contribute to improving safety guidelines and regulatory policies for ultrasound applications in both medical and industrial environments. Understanding the complex interactions between ultrasound waves and biological tissues can aid in developing safer and more effective ultrasound-based therapies, as well as refining workplace exposure limits to ensure occupational health and safety. In conclusion, the review highlights the dual nature of ultrasound waves—both beneficial and potentially harmful depending on the parameters of exposure. Future research should focus on standardizing treatment protocols, optimizing exposure conditions, and investigating long-term effects to ensure safe and effective applications of ultrasound technology across various domains. In occupational settings, prolonged exposure to ultrasonic waves has been associated with potential health risks. Pleban et al. reported that ultrasonic welders and cleaners generate airborne emissions exceeding 100 dB SPL, particularly in the 20–40 kHz range, which may pose auditory and neurological hazards during prolonged exposure [ 14 ]. Applications of ultrasonic waves Ultrasonic waves have widespread applications in various industries. In the food industry [ 46 ], ultrasonic waves are used for cleaning [ 47 ], pasteurization, and extending the shelf life of food products [ 48 – 50 ]. The application of ultrasonic waves in the crystallization process is particularly observed in the chemical and pharmaceutical industries [ 51 ]. In these industries, ultrasound is used to improve crystal quality, accelerate nucleation, and control crystal size [ 52 ]. This technique is especially important in the production of pharmaceuticals and high-purity chemicals [ 53 ], as uniform crystals of the proper size are essential for better product performance. Additionally, in the food industry, ultrasonic waves are employed to enhance the crystallization processes of substances such as sugar and salt [ 54 – 57 ]. In industrial settings, these waves are also used for non-destructive testing, cleaning, and welding [ 58 ]. Ultrasonic waves find applications in esthetic procedures such as skin treatments as well [ 59 , 60 ]. In manufacturing, ultrasound is utilized for plastic welding, material homogenization, and troubleshooting. Professionals from various fields including doctors, physiotherapists, production engineers, and food industry workers (such as chefs, kitchen managers, and quality control technicians) are directly or indirectly involved with ultrasonic waves [ 61 ]. In the medical field, these waves are used for internal imaging, disease diagnosis, physiotherapy treatments, sonophoresis (drug delivery through the skin), dentistry, eye surgery, body shaping, kidney stone fragmentation, and blood clot removal [ 5 ]. For instance, ultrasonography is employed for monitoring pregnancy and examining soft tissues, generally encompassing internal imaging, disease diagnosis, and physiotherapy treatments [ 62 , 63 ]. Furthermore, the biomechanical properties of the femoral heads in patients with osteoporosis can be evaluated using ultrasonic methods. Ultrasonic speeds and elastic moduli increase with frequency, with higher values observed in the axial direction compared to the radial and tangential directions. These findings underscore the importance of ultrasonic methods in diagnosing osteoporosis and predicting the risk of bone fractures (Fig. 2 ) [ 64 ]. This anisotropic behavior is due to the structural orientation of collagen fibers and trabecular alignment in bone, which are more densely packed along the axial direction, resulting in greater stiffness and wave propagation speed. These directional differences are crucial in improving the diagnostic accuracy of ultrasonic methods when assessing osteoporosis-related fracture risk. Other medical applications include the ablation of uterine fibroids, cataract removal (phacoemulsification), surgical tissue cutting and hemostasis, transdermal drug delivery, and aiding in bone fracture repair. Ultrasonic applications continue to expand. Therapeutic applications of ultrasound began before its use in imaging, and various biological effects can occur depending on the exposure levels [ 65 ]. Fig. 2 A commercial LIPUS device for fracture healing (Exogen 4000+, Smith & Nephew, Inc., Memphis, TN, USA) Therapeutic mechanisms of low-intensity ultrasound in bone repair Cellular and molecular mechanisms of LIPUS Ultrasonic waves, particularly low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS), have garnered attention for their regenerative capabilities in bone and bone marrow tissues. LIPUS facilitates fracture healing by promoting osteoblast proliferation, differentiation, and matrix mineralization through activation of signaling pathways involved in osteogenesis [ 20 – 22 ]. These waves also suppress osteoclast activity, enhancing bone formation. Clinical studies typically apply LIPUS at an intensity of 30 mW/cm 2 for 20 min daily, over 2–4 weeks, with consistent acceleration in bone union and reduced recovery times [ 66 , 67 ]. By stimulating cellular responses and mechanical signaling (Fig. 3 ) pathways such as MAPK, acoustic radiation force, and acoustic streaming, LIPUS improves calcium deposition and scaffold integration. Furthermore, it enhances the metabolic activity of bone-forming cells, leading to increased production of ALP, collagen, and osteogenic markers like Osteocalcin (OCN). These mechanisms underpin its utility in accelerating repair processes at the microstructural level [ 23 , 24 , 68 , 69 ]. Fig. 3 Summary of intracellular signaling pathways activated by LIPUS, including MAPK, PI3K/Akt, integrin, and calcium channels [ 25 ] LIPUS effects on bone marrow and stem cells LIPUS enhances the biological activity of BMSCs, increasing their proliferation and promoting their differentiation into osteoblasts rather than osteoclasts [ 69 ]. It contributes to a favorable bone marrow microenvironment by upregulating bone-related proteins such as type I collagen and ALP, and promoting angiogenesis through CD31 expression. These effects are particularly relevant in the context of regenerative medicine. Continued research is required to assess the impact of LIPUS on stem cells from alternative sources such as adipose tissue and its applicability across different skeletal disorders [ 30 ]. In regenerative medicine, recent studies have highlighted the synergistic relationships between ultrasound and other biophysical stimuli, including mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), low-energy laser therapy, and electrical stimulation. LIPUS enhances MSC proliferation, osteogenic differentiation, and extracellular matrix production, similar to the effects observed with low-level laser therapy (LLLT). When used in combination, these modalities can activate overlapping cellular pathways such as the MAPK and PI3K/Akt signaling cascades, amplifying their therapeutic outcomes. Likewise, electrical stimulation has been shown to upregulate osteogenic markers and promote ion channel modulation, which, when paired with ultrasound-induced mechanical stimuli, leads to enhanced tissue regeneration and bone healing. These complementary mechanisms suggest that multimodal approaches integrating LIPUS, MSCs, photobiomodulation, and electrical cues may offer improved clinical efficacy for musculoskeletal repair. Clinical and preclinical evidence on fracture healing Clinical and preclinical studies support the effectiveness of LIPUS in accelerating bone healing. Notably, ultrasound treatment has been associated with a 35–52% increase in fibroblast and osteoblast proliferation and a 112% increase in collagen and non-collagenous protein synthesis, particularly at frequencies such as 45 kHz [ 25 , 26 , 70 ]. Cytokine analysis reveals selective stimulation of IL-1β, VEGF, and IL-8, supporting inflammation modulation and angiogenesis. Recommended intensities include 15–30 mW/cm 2 at 45 kHz and 0.1–0.4 W/cm 2 at 1 MHz, as demonstrated by Guerino et al., who used 30 mW/cm 2 for 5 min daily in a tibial osteotomy mouse model, leading to enhanced bone healing [ 67 ]. Animal model studies demonstrate the synergistic effects of LIPUS and exercise in reducing healing time and improving clinical outcomes. In spinal injury models, LIPUS combined with bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) transplantation improves motor function and tissue reconstruction [ 27 ]. While several clinical and preclinical studies have demonstrated the positive effects of LIPUS on fracture healing and patient recovery, some high-quality randomized controlled trials have reported that LIPUS does not significantly improve radiographic healing outcomes in certain cases, such as fresh fractures [ 71 ]. These discrepancies may be attributed to variations in study design, patient characteristics, fracture type, and treatment protocols. Nevertheless, the overall body of evidence still supports the biological potential of LIPUS, particularly in enhancing cellular responses and accelerating healing in selected clinical contexts. Imaging, diagnostics, and safety considerations LIPUS also serves as a diagnostic tool by providing non-invasive, radiation-free assessment of bone microstructure and architecture. In one study, ultrasonic reflection data showed a strong correlation ( r = 0.87) with CT-based densitometry, demonstrating its potential in early fracture detection and bone health assessment [ 72 , 73 ]. Additionally, LIPUS promotes neovascularization, enhancing blood flow and supporting bone regeneration. Despite its favorable safety profile, standardization of treatment protocols is essential. While clinical evidence supports LIPUS as a valuable adjunct in musculoskeletal medicine, further validation is required to refine regulatory guidelines and optimize patient outcomes [ 28 , 74 ]. Adverse effects of exposure to high-intensity ultrasound or ultrasonic waves Ultrasonic waves can have negative effects on bone and bone marrow. The use of high‐intensity ultrasound may lead to tissue damage, necrosis, cessation of bone healing, and the formation of fibrous tissue. Moreover, diathermy ultrasound treatment can cause localized abnormalities in the bone marrow that resemble the symptoms of osteonecrosis. The heat generated by ultrasonic waves can also damage the surrounding tissues and cause side effects. In general, while ultrasound has therapeutic benefits, improper use or high intensities can lead to serious complications [ 31 , 75 ]. Factors such as exposure duration and wave intensity are among the factors that contribute to tissue damage by ultrasonic waves. If the waves are continuously and immovably concentrated at one point, they can cause localized burns. Also, prolonged use of ultrasonic waves may lead to chromosomal breakage and genetic damage [ 76 ] and, consequently, have genetic effects on future generations. These damages can lead to changes in the genetic structure and potential risks for future generations. Therefore, further research is needed to more deeply examine the biological consequences of exposure to ultrasound [ 77 ]. Research has shown that the use of high‐pressure ultrasonic waves may have more side effects and, in some cases, lead to tissue damage. These waves can cause the production of free radicals and an increase in temperature, which may damage bone tissues [ 73 ]. Various factors can increase the production of free radicals induced by ultrasound. The first factor is the increase in temperature that occurs as a result of exposure to ultrasonic waves (Table 6 ). This temperature increase can lead to the breaking of chemical bonds and the production of free radicals. The second factor is high pressure, which can result in cavitation. This process causes the formation and explosion of gas bubbles in tissue fluids, subsequently producing free radicals. In addition, the duration of exposure to the waves is influential; the longer the exposure, the higher the likelihood of free radical production. Also, the tissue composition and its protein content play an important role in absorbing ultrasonic waves and, as a result, in the production of free radicals. Finally, the presence of chemicals such as carbon dioxide in the environment can also affect the number of free radicals produced; in such a way that the presence of these substances may reduce free radical production. The use of ultrasound in the evaluation of bone and bone marrow diseases may be influenced by the production of free radicals, which in turn is associated with various diseases. These free radicals can lead to tissue damage and inflammation, which play a role in diseases such as osteomyelitis and osteonecrosis. In osteoporosis, increased free radicals can contribute to the degradation of bone tissue and increase the risk of fractures. Also, in diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and Paget’s disease, inflammation due to free radicals can lead to further destruction of bone tissue. Moreover, in conditions where ultrasound is used to stimulate tissue repair, the production of free radicals may negatively affect the healing process. Therefore, monitoring and managing free radical production can be effective in treating and preventing complications arising from bone and bone marrow diseases. In addition, the presence of gas bubbles in tissues can increase the tissues’ sensitivity to the effects of acoustic cavitation. This phenomenon may cause rupture of cell membranes and damage to large molecules. Finally, the presence of intermediary factors such as coupling gel can also affect the transmission of waves, and if not used precisely, can lead to reflection and attenuation of the waves, which in turn can cause tissue damage [ 32 , 78 ]. Due to its non-use of ionizing radiation and low cost, this technique can be a suitable alternative to conventional methods such as X-rays. Ultrasonic waves are sensitive to the microstructure of bone and can provide information about bone architecture that is related to fracture risk [ 26 ]. Various factors can increase the risk of cavitation when using ultrasound. The first factor is high pressure, which can lead to the formation of vapor bubbles in the liquid. Also, a high temperature of the liquid increases vapor pressure and creates conditions for cavitation. The high speed of ultrasonic waves and the short wavelength can also aid in the formation and growth of bubbles. Furthermore, the presence of invisible gas bubbles in solutions and tissues can increase the likelihood of cavitation. Cavitation in bone or bone marrow induced by ultrasonic waves refers to the formation of tiny bubbles filled with gas or vapor in tissue fluids. As mentioned, these bubbles can form due to pressure differences caused by ultrasonic waves and eventually rapidly expand and then collapse. This process results in the production of shock waves, which can lead to mechanical stress and damage. When the gas bubbles collapse, through these shock waves, they may cause abrasion and rupture of the cartilage and bone surfaces and, over time, lead to conditions such as arthritis [ 65 ]. An increase in temperature in the focal area of the ultrasound beam, especially in tissues with high protein content such as bone, can multiply the risk of damage several times. About 70% of the total temperature increase occurs in the first minute of exposure to ultrasound, and this temperature continues to rise with prolonged exposure [ 33 ]. At sound pressure levels (SPL) above 155 decibels, the human body’s temperature can quickly rise to damaging levels. Meanwhile, at levels of 140–150 decibels, only minor heat is observed on the skin. This information indicates that exposure to high‐intensity ultrasound waves can be dangerous and lead to serious damage [ 79 , 80 ]. Another factor contributing to the damage of ultrasonic waves to bone tissue is the intensity of the waves. The higher the intensity, the more energy is produced and, consequently, the more heat and damage are imposed on the bone tissue. The duration of exposure to these waves is also influential; with increased exposure time, more energy is transferred to the tissue. Also, as mentioned, the protein content in bone tissue is a very important factor; tissues with high protein content absorb more energy. The type of frequency and wavelength of the ultrasound also affects the amount of energy; higher frequencies generally produce more energy. Results of a study that examined the negative effects of high‐intensity ultrasonic waves on blood vessels indicate that these waves can cause vasoconstriction and, consequently, reduce blood supply to tissues. This issue particularly affects bone and bone marrow because adequate blood supply is vital for delivering oxygen and nutrients necessary for the proper function of these tissues. Reduced blood flow to bones can lead to serious problems such as avascular necrosis (tissue death due to reduced blood supply). In this case, the bone marrow, which is responsible for producing blood cells, is also affected, and the production of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets may decrease. These disorders can have serious consequences, including anemia, increased risk of infection, and coagulation problems. Therefore, the use of ultrasonic waves in non‐invasive surgeries should be carried out with caution to prevent complications such as vascular spasm and bleeding. These conditions can directly have a negative impact on bone quality and bone marrow function [ 81 ]. To prevent the mechanical effects of ultrasound in bone evaluation, measures can be taken that include precise adjustments and proper use of the device, as well as adjusting the intensity and frequency of the ultrasonic waves (Table 7 ). The use of lower frequencies and lower intensities can help reduce mechanical effects and prevent damage to bone tissues. In addition, using pulsed methods instead of continuous mode can enhance non‐thermal effects and prevent heat accumulation. Also, monitoring the treatment duration and moving the transducer during treatment can help reduce damage caused by cavitation and mechanical pressure (Table 5 ). Finally, training physiotherapists to recognize the specific conditions of the patient and adjust appropriate treatment protocols can also help reduce complications arising from ultrasound [ 65 ]. Audible noise generated by ultrasonic devices, particularly in industrial settings, is increasingly recognized as a potential health hazard. Studies have shown that prolonged exposure to frequencies near or within the audible range (10–20 kHz) may lead to auditory discomfort, stress, and in some cases, hearing-related symptoms [ 14 , 82 ]. Table 6 summarizes the multifactorial causes of tissue temperature elevation during ultrasound exposure. This increase in temperature results from both ultrasound parameters (e.g., frequency, pulse duration, intensity) and intrinsic tissue characteristics (e.g., attenuation, absorption coefficient, perfusion rate). These interactions play a pivotal role in the formation of free radicals and subsequent biological effects. For instance, higher intensity or longer exposure time can elevate local temperature, which may lead to the breakdown of molecular bonds and free radical generation. Moreover, the role of cavitation, especially under high-pressure conditions further contributes to the mechanical stress and potential tissue damage observed with certain ultrasound protocols. Understanding these parameters is essential for optimizing therapeutic outcomes while minimizing potential risks. High vs. low-intensity ultrasound: unraveling their differential effects on bone and bone marrow Ultrasound can be broadly categorized according to acoustic intensity (typically expressed as intensity (W/cm 2 ), rather than frequency alone) into low-intensity and high-intensity modalities. The low-intensity group includes physiotherapy, fracture repair, and sonophoresis [ 2 ], while HIFU has applications in industries as well as various applications in the medical field [ 46 , 49 , 56 , 62 ]. Low-power ultrasound has beneficial and reversible cellular effects, whereas high-power ultrasound, in fact, aims at immediate cell death [ 65 ]. In general, ultrasonic waves can affect bone and bone marrow in two ways: damage and repair. At high frequencies, HIFU may impair blood flow to bone tissues, contributing to necrosis and marrow dysfunction. In contrast, LIPUS at frequencies of 1–3 MHz is capable of positively influencing bone repair [ 34 ]. This type of ultrasound stimulates the activity of bone-forming cells (osteoblasts) and accelerates biological processes such as increased mineralization and tissue repair [ 83 ]. Continuous exposure to low-frequency ultrasound at a pressure level of 20 kilopascals (180 decibels), even for 1 min, can be lethal and lead to complete destruction of blood cells [ 84 ]. It is important to clarify that “low-frequency ultrasound” is not synonymous with “low-intensity ultrasound” (LIPUS). Frequency refers to the number of oscillations per second, while intensity denotes the energy transmitted per unit area. Although low-intensity ultrasound is widely used for therapeutic purposes and is considered safe, low-frequency ultrasound delivered at extremely high pressures (such as 20 kPa) can be lethal. The harmful effects in this context are due to the high acoustic pressure, which can induce cavitation and cellular destruction—not due to low-intensity therapeutic use. LIPUS can help increase the activity of key enzymes such as alkaline phosphatase and collagen synthesis, which are essential for bone repair [ 35 ]. According to Table 7 , intensity and exposure parameters vary by application. Therapeutic devices typically operate at 0.03–0.1 W/cm 2 for 15–30 min daily, while industrial HIFU systems may exceed 5 W/cm 2 in short pulses lasting only seconds. Safety in ultrasonic wave applications Given the presence of ultrasonic devices in various industries such as pharmaceuticals, food, medicine, automotive, and industrial production, employees may be directly or indirectly exposed to ultrasound waves [ 85 , 86 ]. This exposure can pose health risks, particularly regarding bone tissue injuries. Exposure to ultrasound waves can lead to thermal and mechanical changes in tissues, which may result in tissue damage, including damage to bones and bone marrow, depending on the type and intensity of these waves [ 12 ]. Long-term use of LIPUS is generally safe, but under certain conditions, it may cause harm. Influential factors include the duration and intensity of exposure, the presence of damaged tissue, and the specific condition of the individual being exposed. Therefore, monitoring the duration and intensity of treatment and consulting a physician to prevent side effects is essential. This information is derived from various studies on the effects of LIPUS on bone healing [ 21 , 26 , 36 ]. Based on the biophysical effects in ultrasonography, which provides a rationale for the Mechanical Index (MI) and Thermal Index (TI) that align with the Output Display Standard (ODS), safe doses of ultrasonography are determined based on specific regulations, and the values related to MI and TI are displayed on the screen (Fig. 4 ). These indices address the physical mechanisms of interaction between ultrasonic waves and biological tissues and depend on the temporal and spatial parameters of the acoustic field generated by ultrasonic transducers. The predicted temperature rise is determined using three different tissue models, including homogeneous, layered, and bone/tissue interface models. At higher frequencies, ultrasonic waves can cause an increase in temperature in tissues, especially in bone, which has a high absorption coefficient. This temperature increase may lead to tissue damage and serious problems such as necrosis. Similarly, using ultrasonography with an appropriate intensity and adhering to MI and TI limits can aid in tissue repair. Therefore, the correct choice of the type and intensity of ultrasonography is very important to prevent negative effects and facilitate the healing process [ 87 ]. The use of ultrasound in bone evaluation also involves specific safety limitations. One of these limitations is burning, which may occur if waves are used continuously and without movement at a single point. The thermal effects of these waves can lead to necrosis and apoptosis of cells, thereby negatively affecting normal bone function. Therefore, comprehensive research to identify the risks arising from exposure to these waves in various occupations is necessary. Increasing public awareness about the harmful effects of these waves and preventive strategies can help protect workers’ health and improve the quality of life for those exposed [ 88 – 90 ]. Additionally, the creation of cavities or cavitation can lead to tissue damage and biological changes such as cell membrane rupture. Furthermore, the use of high-power ultrasound waves may cause chromosomal breakage and DNA damage. Also, in certain areas such as tissues with active infection, cancerous tumors, or implants, ultrasound should be used with caution to avoid side effects [ 37 , 77 ]. Ultrasonic waves can negatively impact bone and bone marrow. Localized abnormalities in the bone marrow of patients who have undergone ultrasonic diathermy have been observed. These abnormalities may resemble the symptoms of bone necrosis, indicating the negative thermal effects of these waves on sensitive tissues [ 26 ]. Moreover, ultrasonic waves can affect biological processes such as mineralization and collagen formation, which may result in reduced bone quality and an increased risk of fractures. Although the use of ultrasonic techniques in medicine is considered safe, following the necessary precautions and limitations to prevent potential complications is essential [ 91 ]. Concerns about the safety of these waves have led various organizations to set limits on the output intensity of ultrasonic devices. Although the use of ultrasonic waves in medicine is generally considered safe, adhering to the limits set by regulatory bodies such as the FDA is necessary to prevent potential complications. These measures include controlling the devices’ output intensity and monitoring temperature and mechanical effects caused by the waves [ 38 ]. Protection against improper or hazardous ultrasonic exposure is governed by international standards and national regulations. IEC 60601 Part 1 establishes mechanical, electrical, chemical, and thermal safety requirements for all electromedical equipment. In Part 2 of this standard, for diagnostic ultrasonic equipment, no limits are specified for ultrasonic exposure; rather, safety indices are defined to guide users regarding thermal and mechanical risks [ 16 ]. Education and awareness about the safe use of ultrasonic devices and their effects on bone health are very important so that employees can take preventive measures to avoid serious injuries. Adhering to safety protocols, controlling exposure, and using appropriate equipment by trained professionals can reduce the risks associated with exposure to ultrasound waves [ 82 ]. In various industries, there are multiple methods for protection against ultrasound waves. The use of protective equipment such as safety glasses, gloves, and specialized clothing can help prevent direct contact with the waves [ 92 ]. Additionally, training employees about potential hazards and safe usage of ultrasound equipment is highly effective. Designing ultrasound devices to emit the lowest possible energy in non-essential areas is of great importance. Using high-precision transducers that emit energy in a focused manner can reduce risks. Furthermore, to prevent thermal damage, cold water or cooling gels can be used near the skin to control temperature and prevent tissue damage. Adjusting parameters such as frequency and ultrasound emission time can also help reduce negative effects. Monitoring temperature during treatment using imaging techniques like MR thermometry can aid in regulating therapeutic energy and preventing thermal damage [ 93 ]. These methods help reduce the risks posed by ultrasound waves in industrial and clinical settings, thereby increasing safety for workers and patients. Fig. 4 Key parameters influencing TI and MI include PRF (pulse repetition frequency) [ 38 ] Needs for enhanced safety and alternatives to ultrasonic waves Limitations on the use of ultrasound in bone evaluation depend on several factors. Firstly, ultrasound waves cannot pass well through tissues containing air or gas; therefore, they are less effective in examining gas-filled tissues such as the lungs and intestines. Secondly, ultrasound is only capable of evaluating the surfaces of bones and cannot provide accurate information about the internal structure of the bone. Additionally, in obese individuals, ultrasound waves do not easily penetrate deep tissues, which can lead to reduced image quality. Finally, there is also the possibility of side effects resulting from thermal and mechanical effects, which can impose limitations on the use of this method [ 32 , 94 ]. The speed of ultrasound wave propagation in the body decreases with increasing age of the individual, especially after menopause [ 95 ]. It should be noted that the use of ultrasound waves in the treatment of bone fractures, especially in different age groups, yields varied results [ 74 ]. Included studies suggest that ultrasound-based interventions may be beneficial in certain fracture contexts, with outcomes varying by exposure parameters and study conditions. Hence, adherence to safety standards and further research to determine optimal parameters is essential in order to exploit the benefits of this technology without causing serious health risks [ 96 ]. Ultrasonic technologies such as QUS (Quantitative Ultrasound) are recognized as effective tools for evaluating bone health and predicting fracture risk. Although more than 20 years have passed since the first recorded use of QUS for predicting bone fragility, this field has not yet reached maturity [ 39 , 97 ]. QUS has the potential to predict fracture risk in various clinical conditions and offers advantages such as the absence of ionizing radiation, low cost, portability, and high repeatability. However, the expansion of QUS in clinical practice is limited, and there is no clinical consensus on how to integrate QUS technologies into bone density measurement tools. Critical issues such as appropriate technologies for measuring the central skeleton, data collection, and signal processing must be resolved for the role of QUS in rheumatology to be developed [ 98 ]. This emphasis on rheumatology reflects the increasing clinical interest in using QUS to monitor systemic bone changes in chronic inflammatory diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis, which are traditionally managed within the field of rheumatology. Nevertheless, QUS applications are also highly relevant to orthopedics, particularly in fracture risk assessment and bone quality evaluation. In the study by Laugier in 2008, the latest technological advances in in vivo bone strength assessment were examined, and measurement and signal processing methods were described. Current limitations, especially the lack of standardization and the shortage of comprehensive theoretical models, were also highlighted, and suggestions were provided for technological challenges and future research areas [ 95 , 97 , 99 , 100 ]. The skull vibrations produced by the UBC (unfused bone center) device are significantly smaller than the vibrations produced by traditional high-speed drills in frequencies ranging from 500 to 8000 Hz. This feature enables UBC to be safely used in non-invasive surgeries such as TEES (transcanal endoscopic ear surgery) without posing a risk of damage to the inner ear. Therefore, the correct selection of the type and intensity of ultrasound is crucial for preventing negative side effects and facilitating repair processes, and it can play an important role in improving bone health [ 101 , 102 ]. Alternative methods for treating bone and bone marrow, apart from ultrasonic waves, include innovative techniques that can have positive effects on tissue repair and improvement. These methods have gained attention due to advantages such as reduced side effects, increased efficiency, and improved therapeutic outcomes compared to traditional treatments. One of these methods is the use of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) for tissue and bone repair. Additionally, tissue engineering technologies, which involve combining cells with scaffolds to create new tissues, are also applied in this field. Low-energy laser therapy for stimulating tissue repair is another such method. Furthermore, new drug therapies that can accelerate the repair process, as well as electrical stimulation that uses electrical currents to promote bone growth, are among the treatment options. Physiotherapy and rehabilitation exercises also contribute to improved function and accelerated repair through controlled movements. In general, these methods, due to their ability to reduce side effects and increase the speed of repair, can be suitable options for patients [ 103 ]. Bone evaluation mainly relies on standard methods such as radiography, CT scan, MRI, and bone scanning, which vary depending on the complexity of the anatomical region and the clinical condition. Due to the difference in acoustic impedance between soft tissues and the bone cortex, ultrasound only allows for the evaluation of bone surfaces. However, ultrasound can be useful in evaluating various bone disorders in limbs and, owing to its tomographic capabilities and high resolution, provides valuable information [ 99 , 100 ]. Based on moderate to high-quality evidence from studies on patients with fresh fractures, the use of LIPUS does not appear to significantly improve patient outcomes and is unlikely to affect the radiographic healing of bone [ 104 ]. Here, moderate to high-quality evidence refers to findings derived primarily from randomized controlled trials with low risk of bias and consistent results, interpreted using established evidence-rating frameworks [ 71 ]. This raises concerns about the application of LIPUS in other types of fractures or bone procedures. While some preliminary studies have shown positive results, further investigations are needed to confirm the efficacy of this method in various conditions, and physicians should exercise greater caution when deciding to use LIPUS [ 71 ]. The use of LIPUS may reduce the time to radiographic union of a fracture, but this does not guarantee functional improvement or prevention of delayed healing. The increased bone formation induced by LIPUS may be a valuable tool in fracture repair, but it does not always lead to recovery. Why isn’t LIPUS always an effective method for treating bone and bone marrow? This is because clinical and radiographic outcomes alone cannot demonstrate treatment efficacy. Furthermore, LIPUS may have a lesser effect in specific conditions or certain types of fractures, and further research is needed to examine its effects on clinical indicators, functional recovery, and radiographic union [ 100 , 105 ]. To ensure that the benefits of ultrasonic treatments outweigh their risks, attention must be paid to the standardization, dosing of ultrasound, and the reduction of side effects. Therapeutic ultrasound typically provides a manageable safety profile for physicians because its benefits and risks are well defined. However, it should be noted that safety information may be fragmented or influenced by commercial interests. Effective communication of safety information is crucial to address these challenges. Reputable organizations, such as the American Institute of Ultrasound in Medicine, play an important role in disseminating practical safety guidelines to the medical community. The Bioeffects Committee at this institute identifies the various ultrasonic therapeutic methods that are currently in clinical use or under study and provides guidance to ensure the safety of therapeutic ultrasound. In summary, while therapeutic ultrasound has been beneficial in a wide range of medical applications, it is essential that its benefits are balanced with its potential risks. Continuous research and adherence to safety protocols will help optimize patient outcomes and enhance the efficacy of ultrasound as a therapeutic tool [ 10 , 13 ]. Discussion Integrated synthesis Although prior studies have independently explored either the therapeutic or occupational aspects of ultrasound, this review provides a unique integrative synthesis across these domains. Overall, the evidence supports a parameter-dependent duality: under controlled low-intensity conditions, ultrasound can promote regenerative responses in skeletal tissues, whereas higher-intensity or poorly controlled exposures, particularly in industrial settings, may induce thermal or mechanical bioeffects. This dual perspective also highlights inconsistencies in safety practices and reporting standards that may limit cross-context comparability and hinder evidence translation. QUS Quantitative ultrasound (QUS) has emerged as a complementary tool for skeletal assessment and fracture risk estimation. Glüer et al. demonstrated that QUS parameters—such as ultrasound velocity in bone (UVB) and broadband ultrasound attenuation (BUA)—correlate independently with trabecular bone structure, regardless of bone mineral density [ 39 ]. Despite this diagnostic potential, broader clinical adoption remains limited by device variability, lack of standardization, and methodological differences in acquisition and signal processing, highlighting the need for harmonized protocols and validation studies. Therapeutic (LIPUS) with plausibility Therapeutically, LIPUS (low-intensity pulsed ultrasound) has shown promise in modulating cellular behavior and accelerating tissue repair. Wu et al., in a mouse model of orthodontic movement, showed that LIPUS mitigated bone loss and enhanced osteogenic markers Collagen Type I (COL1) and osteocalcin (OCN) suppressed by compressive forces. These effects were attributed to modulation of the cytoskeleton–Lamin A/C–YAP signaling axis [ 40 ]. Similarly, Yang et al. reported that LIPUS enhanced osteoblast function by upregulating osteogenic genes such as Runx2 and Dlx5, suggesting its utility in bone regeneration [ 41 ]. The synergistic use of LIPUS and physical exercise has also drawn attention. Guerino et al. and Claes and Willie both used a mouse tibial osteotomy model to evaluate the combined effects of LIPUS and exercise on bone fracture healing. They found that daily 5-min LIPUS treatment accelerated early bone repair, while swimming exercise with a 5% body weight load enhanced muscle glycogen reserves. When combined, these interventions stimulated molecular changes that promoted faster recovery and improved clinical outcomes [ 66 , 67 ]. These results provide compelling evidence that mechanical stimulation can complement acoustic interventions in orthopedics. Collectively, these preclinical findings support biological plausibility for LIPUS-induced osteogenesis; however, translation to consistent clinical benefit likely depends on fracture context, dosing parameters, and outcome selection. Sources of heterogeneity and conflicting evidence Notably, clinical outcomes are not uniformly consistent across fracture contexts. Differences in fracture type (fresh vs. delayed/nonunion), patient characteristics, treatment compliance, and ultrasound dose parameters (intensity, duty cycle, application time, and treatment duration) likely contribute to the mixed evidence base. Moreover, reliance on radiographic endpoints alone may not capture patient-important outcomes such as pain reduction, functional recovery, and complication rates, which may partly explain why improvements in radiographic union do not always translate into clinically meaningful benefits. Therefore, the apparent variability in LIPUS effectiveness is plausibly driven by clinical heterogeneity and methodological variability, rather than a single uniform biological response. In particular, high-quality randomized evidence in fresh fractures has frequently shown no clinically meaningful improvement in radiographic healing or patient-important outcomes, despite biological plausibility observed in preclinical models [ 71 ]. For example, in a large randomized controlled trial on fresh tibial fractures, postoperative LIPUS did not improve functional recovery, with a small and clinically insignificant difference in SF-36 physical component scores (mean difference 0.55; 95% CI −0.75 to 1.84), nor did it accelerate radiographic healing (hazard ratio 1.07; 95% CI 0.86–1.34) compared with sham treatment [ 104 ]. Safety + occupational + practical implications However, safety concerns remain. Barnett et al. emphasized the need for regulated use of modern high-output ultrasound devices, warning that without adherence to ALARA principles (As Low As Reasonably Achievable), users may inadvertently induce thermal or mechanical tissue damage [ 106 ]. In addition, undesirable side effects may also be associated with these treatments. For example, thermal therapies can lead to burns, while mechanical treatments such as lithotripsy can cause severe bleeding [ 10 ]. Accordingly, therapeutic ultrasound exposure should be applied under controlled conditions and within established safety limits to minimize adverse effects. Prolonged exposure at certain frequencies and intensities has been associated with tissue injury and, in occupational contexts, hearing-related effects. Industrial contexts present additional risks. Cieslak et al. and Pleban et al. highlighted occupational exposures to harmful ultrasonic noise from equipment like welders and cleaners, suggesting that current monitoring practices may underestimate risk levels [ 14 , 82 ]. Biological tissue damage under excessive exposure was confirmed by Delius et al., who documented hemorrhagic and periosteal injuries following focused shock wave application in rabbits, suggesting cavitation as the likely mechanism [ 107 ]. Stratmeyer et al. demonstrated that pulsed ultrasound can induce biological tissue damage through non-thermal mechanisms, particularly at intensities significantly higher than those used in clinical diagnostics, and especially in the absence of gas bodies [ 42 ]. Similarly, Church and Miller (2006) highlighted that biomedical ultrasound may cause both thermal and non-thermal effects, such as heat-induced teratogenesis and vascular damage, particularly near developing bones. They further noted that diagnostic ultrasound could increase fetal activity, although harmful effects generally occur at exposures exceeding FDA regulatory limits. Despite these concerns, low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS) remains a clinically accepted modality due to its proven benefits in enhancing fracture healing, soft tissue regeneration, and neural repair in both preclinical and clinical settings. These contrasting findings emphasize the critical importance of intensity control and adherence to safety standards to ensure effective yet non-harmful application of ultrasound technologies [ 42 , 83 ]. The biological effects of ultrasound exposure are highly dependent on the acoustic intensity used. Low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS), typically <0.1 W/cm 2 , has shown beneficial effects in bone regeneration and stem cell modulation with minimal side effects. In contrast, high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU), often exceeding 5 W/cm 2 , is associated with thermal necrosis and hemorrhagic effects in therapeutic ablation. Industrial ultrasound applications, operating in a moderate intensity range (1–10 W/cm 2 ), have been linked to localized heating, microcracks, or mechanical strain in tissues during long-term exposure. These findings emphasize that appropriate intensity selection is essential for maximizing therapeutic outcomes while minimizing unintended damage across different fields of application [ 14 , 42 , 106 ]. Conclusion This systematic review summarizes current evidence on the biomechanical and biological effects of ultrasound exposure on bone and bone marrow across clinical, industrial, and laboratory contexts. Overall, the findings indicate that ultrasound effects are strongly dependent on exposure parameters, especially acoustic intensity and treatment conditions. Controlled low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS) is generally associated with regenerative cellular responses and may support fracture healing in selected settings, whereas higher-intensity or poorly controlled exposures (including HIFU and certain industrial sources) may produce harmful thermal or mechanical effects, such as tissue injury and impaired skeletal function. Importantly, clinical results are not uniform across fracture types, and improvements in radiographic outcomes do not always translate into patient-important benefits. The reviewed literature also reveals gaps in standardized reporting and inconsistencies in safety practices between medical and occupational environments. These findings highlight the need for clearer safety standards, better monitoring of exposure, and more consistent outcome reporting to support safe and effective use of ultrasound in skeletal applications. documents.title: Diagnosis, prevention and treatment of common shoulder injuries in sport: grading the evidence - a statement paper commissioned by the Danish Society of Sports Physical Therapy (DSSF).
documents.abstract: This statement paper summarises and appraises the evidence on diagnosis, prevention, and treatment of common shoulder injuries in sports. We systematically searched Medline and Embase. The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation tool was applied to evaluate the overall quality of evidence.For diagnosis, we included 19 clinical tests from mixed populations. Tests for anterior instability, biceps-labrum complex injuries and full subscapularis rupture had high diagnostic accuracy (low to moderate quality of evidence).For prevention, the Oslo Sports Trauma Research Center, the Shoulder Control, the FIFA 11+ shoulder injury prevention programmes, and a baseball-specific programme (range of motion, stretching, dynamic stability and strengthening exercises) showed moderate to large effect size in reducing the risk of shoulder injury compared with no intervention (very low to moderate quality of evidence).For treatment, a rehabilitation programme including stretching, ice packs, electrotherapy and compression, and strengthening exercises showed a large effect size in reducing pain and disability compared with no intervention in athletes with subacromial impingement syndrome (very low to moderate quality of evidence). For the treatment of supraspinatus tendinopathy, hyperthermia treatment (heating the skin to 38°C-40°C) resulted in large effect size in reducing pain and disability compared with ultrasound or pendular swinging and stretching exercises (moderate quality of evidence). Strengthening exercise alone or in combination with stretching exercises promoted a large effect in reducing shoulder pain (cohort studies, no comparators) (very low quality of evidence). The quality of evidence for most estimates was low to moderate, indicating that future high-quality research may alter our recommendations for clinical practice.

Abstract This statement paper summarises and appraises the evidence on diagnosis, prevention, and treatment of common shoulder injuries in sports. We systematically searched Medline and Embase. The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation tool was applied to evaluate the overall quality of evidence. For diagnosis, we included 19 clinical tests from mixed populations. Tests for anterior instability, biceps-labrum complex injuries and full subscapularis rupture had high diagnostic accuracy (low to moderate quality of evidence). For prevention, the Oslo Sports Trauma Research Center, the Shoulder Control, the FIFA 11+ shoulder injury prevention programmes, and a baseball-specific programme (range of motion, stretching, dynamic stability and strengthening exercises) showed moderate to large effect size in reducing the risk of shoulder injury compared with no intervention (very low to moderate quality of evidence). For treatment, a rehabilitation programme including stretching, ice packs, electrotherapy and compression, and strengthening exercises showed a large effect size in reducing pain and disability compared with no intervention in athletes with subacromial impingement syndrome (very low to moderate quality of evidence). For the treatment of supraspinatus tendinopathy, hyperthermia treatment (heating the skin to 38°C–40°C) resulted in large effect size in reducing pain and disability compared with ultrasound or pendular swinging and stretching exercises (moderate quality of evidence). Strengthening exercise alone or in combination with stretching exercises promoted a large effect in reducing shoulder pain (cohort studies, no comparators) (very low quality of evidence). The quality of evidence for most estimates was low to moderate, indicating that future high-quality research may alter our recommendations for clinical practice.
